_about: THE DECISION LOG — the source. MoneyKeel/documents/decision-log/moneykeel_log_decisions_v01.xlsx is PRINTED from this by build-decision-log.py; a hand edit to the workbook dies on the next build. Founder, 2026-09-28: one place for every decision, no matter where it was made. A decision identifier is issued once and never re-pointed. A row is never deleted — a reversed decision is SUPERSEDED and says by what.

rows.his_words: What if I save more?
rows.plain:
The Look ahead screen — “What if I save more?” — was redrawn. Three decisions:
1. Your age and the age you plan to retire are set with sliders on the screen itself, not on a separate page, and they save to the same two answers the rest of the app reads.
2. The difference the extra saving makes, and the projected nest egg, each carry a tappable “i” that explains where the figure comes from.
3. The screen no longer asks you to fill in your plan first before it will show you anything.
rows.means: What-if (Look ahead) redesigned: inline age + retire-at sliders saved to canonical fields (birthYear, retirementAssumptions.retireAge); info dots on the delta and Projected nest egg with the estimate explanation; plan-basics empty state removed; title "What if I save more?"
rows.why: Founder direction during Build-43 review: reduce friction — user enters information on the screen instead of Home → Sharpen your plan → …; no duplicate fields.

rows.his_words: Which 12 months are you entering?
rows.plain:
When you enter a year of income, the app asks which twelve months you mean — the calendar year, or the next twelve months from now. Three decisions:
1. Every month you enter carries its own month AND year, so entering across a New Year does not overwrite the wrong month.
2. Both ways of asking write to the same twelve calendar slots underneath, so the answer means the same thing however it was entered.
3. When a receipt is scanned, the total is read from the total — never from a line about how it was paid, which is not what you spent.
rows.means: Income pop-up (v2): "Which 12 months are you entering?" — Calendar year N or Next 12 months; every month chip and editor carries month + year (incl. across the New-Year boundary); both frames write the same canonical calendar slots; note "this yearly pattern repeats". Receipt scanning: totals never read from payment-mechanics lines.
rows.why: Founder Build-44 findings (rows 33-34)

rows.his_words: "yes" — DEC-0019, confirmed as written: B47 FINDING 3 FIXED (Vanguard): balance authority rule gains the derive-from-holdings fallback when the broker reports n
rows.plain:
When you link a brokerage, the app takes the account's total straight from the broker. Vanguard sent back no total at all, while the account really held $132,000 — so it showed $0. Four decisions:
1. When the broker gives no total, or gives zero, add up EVERYTHING THE ACCOUNT HOLDS instead: every holding in it at today's price — stocks, ETFs, funds, bonds, CDs, Treasuries — plus any options, plus the uninvested cash sitting in it. Not just the shares: an account is whatever is in it.
2. Where a holding has no price, use what was paid for it — never nothing, because a holding priced at zero would quietly shrink your whole net worth.
3. If the broker DOES send a real total, that still wins. We only add it up ourselves when there is nothing usable to take.
4. Only for accounts held in US dollars, and an account that is genuinely empty stays at zero. A foreign-currency account's holdings are priced in that currency, so adding them up would produce a dollar figure that is not real; and an empty account is empty, not unknown.
rows.means: B47 FINDING 3 FIXED (Vanguard): balance authority rule gains the derive-from-holdings fallback when the broker reports no usable total (missing/zero) — marks + options + cash sleeve; USD-only (currency guard); empty stays zero; real totals still win. 3 new ingest pins.

rows.plain:
One debt editor, not two, and it changes shape according to how the debt is repaid. Three shapes:
1. A loan with fixed payments asks for the payment OR the date it will be paid off — each works out the other.
2. A credit card asks for the minimum and what you actually pay.
3. A debt due in one lump asks for the amount and the date, and that then appears in cash flow and on the bill calendar as a dated bill. This replaces two debt forms that had drifted apart.
rows.means: ONE debt editor shaped by repayment (installment: real payment ↔ paid-off-by; cards: min + you-pay; due in full: amount + date → dated big-ticket in cash flow + bill calendar). Replaces the two drifted debt forms.

rows.plain:
Three decisions about the Net worth screen:
1. The By type view is REMOVED, which settles the open question about it.

rows.plain:

rows.means: Retirement verdict wording: working = "Likely — retire at {65} with ~{pot at retirement}, lasting past {92} with ~{leftover} to spare"; retired = "Holding — on course to last past {92}, ~{leftover} to spare". Renders nothing when data is complete. 7 engine pins + 1 screen pin.

rows.plain: A broken connection now says it is broken. A failure on one account was being noted only in the developer log, so a dead connection and a healthy quiet one looked identical — same “connected” label, same unchanging date. Failures are now recorded against the account and shown.
rows.means: A DEAD CONNECTION CAN NOW SAY IT IS DEAD. Per-account sync failures were caught and only console-warned, so a broken connection and a healthy idle one looked identical — same "connected" label, same unchanging date. rows.his_words: Vanguard -5738
rows.plain:
His refinement of the account-naming rule, recorded in the requirements. Three decisions:
1. A taxable account is the institution plus the last four digits — “Vanguard -5738”.
2. With no digits it is the institution plus the kind of account — “Vanguard Brokerage”, “Chase Checking”, “Ally Savings”.
3. Two accounts that would read the same are numbered, so no two rows are indistinguishable.
rows.means: THE NAMING RULE REFINED BY THE FOUNDER AND RECORDED IN THE PRD: (1) TAXABLE accounts = institution + last four ("Vanguard -5738"); with no digits = institution + the account word ("Vanguard Brokerage", "Chase Checking", "Ally Savings"); duplicates get · 1 / · 2. (2) TAX-ADVANTAGED accounts = institution + wrapper + last four when available ("Vanguard Roth IRA -5738"), because the wrapper IS the tax treatment; without digits "Fidelity 401(k)". A kind that describes HOLDINGS (stocks_etf, crypto, fixed_income, options) names the ACCOUNT that holds them — Brokerage — via a new wrapperWord map, so the row never reads "Vanguard Stocks / ETFs". Saved to the master requirements file: PRD v1.1 Amendments tab + a new Sameness-contract row naming the canonical helper and its pinning test.
rows.why: Founder rule 2026-08-11, refining the same-day first pass. It resolves the open question I raised: the wrapper carries the tax treatment, so it is compulsory exactly where tax treatment differs and optional where the digits already identify the account.

rows.his_words: Your retirement plan - it says See your plan. That is not what I approved. Is it stale code?
rows.plain: The retirement card must give you its verdict even when the news is bad. It used to show nothing below an 80% chance, so both Net worth and the Plan screen fell back to a bare “See your plan” — the app went silent at exactly the moment you needed telling.
rows.means: THE RETIREMENT CARD NO LONGER GOES QUIET WHEN THE NEWS IS BAD. onCourseSentence returned null below 80% odds, so both the Net worth card and the Plan hub fell back to a bare "See your plan ›" — the founder saw this on device and asked whether it was stale code. It was not: it was a deliberate gate that silenced the verdict exactly when it mattered. The verdict words themselves prove the design meant to speak in every case (Likely / Uncertain / Unlikely; Holding / Watch closely / Running short). The sentence now renders for EVERY computable plan, and the ending tells the truth: "lasting past 92 with ~$890,000 to spare" only when there IS something spare, otherwise "running short around age 84" — the age read from the band the simulation already produces (new shortfallAgeFromBand helper, wired on both screens). It stays silent only when there is genuinely nothing to say: no odds yet, or no projected pot.
rows.why: Founder device finding 2026-08-11: "Your retirement plan - it says See your plan. That is not what I approved. Is it stale code?" The approved card shows a verdict word plus the plan; a fallback that hides both was never approved.

rows.his_words: where are we getting data or assumptions for monte carlo simulation?
rows.plain: How much your investments swing up and down is now measured from what you actually hold, instead of being guessed from the return. The old rule of thumb called a savings account 5% volatile and could not tell the difference between bonds and shares — which makes the odds meaningless.
rows.means: PORTFOLIO RISK IS NOW MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. The Monte Carlo used volatility = return × 1.7 (floored at 5%), a rule of thumb that called a savings account 5% volatile and could not express that bonds and shares swing differently. New KIND_VOLATILITY table = the annual standard deviation of each asset kind, drawn from the SAME long-run series as the returns, each with a named source in VOLATILITY_META (S&P 500 for shares, US Aggregate for bonds, T-bills for cash, Case-Shiller for property; crypto/PE/hedge flagged as estimates). blendedVolatility weights them the way the money actually sits — the same weighting blendedReturn uses — so the return and the risk always describe ONE portfolio. Weighted-average volatility assumes the parts move together, which slightly OVERSTATES risk; erring cautious rather than flattering is the right side. The old return×1.7 rule survives only as the scenario fallback, for when someone types a return on the Plan sliders with nothing held yet.
rows.why: Founder question 2026-08-11: "where are we getting data or assumptions for monte carlo simulation?" — I flagged the derived volatility as the weakest assumption and the founder asked for it to be fixed.

rows.plain: The cash-means-cash rule now holds where accounts are classified as they arrive, not only in the one-off tidy-up of existing data. A holding was being classed purely by the tag the broker sends, and brokers tag both money-market funds and CDs as cash — so a position added after the tidy-up landed back in Cash. The same defect as the original, mirrored in time.
rows.means: THE 2026-08-04 RULE NOW HOLDS AT THE LIVE CLASSIFICATION POINT, not only in the one-time migration. (a) accountClassBreakdown classified a POSITION purely by the tag the broker sends — and brokers tag both money-market funds and CDs as "cash" — so a holding synced AFTER the migration ran landed straight back in Cash. That is the founder's original CD-under-Cash defect mirrored in time (old data fixed, new data not). The name/ticker rule is applied at classification now, so it holds whenever the data arrives. (b) The rule matched on the fund NAME, so a broker sending only a symbol (VMFXX, SPAXX, SWVXX…) still put its money-market fund in Cash — the founder's own gap #2 surviving in the one place a name never appears. A list of the widely-held money-market symbols at Vanguard, Fidelity, Schwab, Merrill, BlackRock and Goldman now backs the name rule. ALSO: the account sub-line no longer names money-market funds under Cash at all — a cash slice is the sweep balance, so it reads "cash in this account". A stale 2026-07-19 test that asserted VMFXX belonged in Cash was corrected with the reason.
rows.why: Founder correction 2026-08-11: "we decided to move money markets and T-bills to stock/etf and bond & CD respectively." Checking the copy against the rule exposed two places the rule was not actually being applied.

rows.his_words: make all $$ same size and make totals bold. different size for dollar amount makes number not right aligned... are these tables or how are you ensuring they are right aligned?
rows.plain: Two decisions: every money figure on the screen is the same size, with totals in bold — section totals were smaller than the rows beneath them, so a total read as less important than its parts. And every number shares one true right-hand edge, totals included.
rows.means: ONE SIZE FOR EVERY MONEY FIGURE, AND A REAL RIGHT EDGE. (a) Band totals rendered at 13pt while row values rendered at 15pt; every money figure is 15pt now, totals bold, so a band total and the rows beneath it read as one column. SectionBand is shared, so this lands on every banded screen. (b) THE COLUMN WAS GENUINELY BENT, and the founder was right to doubt it: a ledger ROW lays out [name][gap 8][value][gap 8][arrow 16], so its value ends 36pt from the screen edge, while a BAND placed its total at padding + 16 = 28pt. Band totals sat 8 points right of every row value. One constant (RIGHT_SLOT = arrow + gap) is now what every band passes, so both end on the same line by construction. (c) The test that was supposed to guard this only asserted marginRight === 16 — necessary and not sufficient, and it never compared the two sides. It now COMPUTES the distance from the screen edge to each number's right edge and asserts equality, plus that every money figure is one size and totals are bold.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-11: "make all $$ same size and make totals bold. different size for dollar amount makes number not right aligned... are these tables or how are you ensuring they are right aligned?" — the question exposed a real 8-point misalignment and a test that could not have caught it.

rows.his_words: why is cash added to CD and not cash?
rows.plain: When a broker’s stated total is more than the holdings it listed, the difference is treated as CASH — not added to the largest holding. On a CD-heavy account the old rule silently inflated the CDs by money that was really sitting uninvested.
rows.means: THE LEFTOVER IS CASH, NOT MORE OF THE BIGGEST HOLDING. When a broker's stated account total exceeded the sum of the holdings it itemised, the difference was added to the LARGEST class — so on a CD-heavy account the uninvested money was counted as MORE CDs, overstating the bonds slice and understating cash, silently, up to 1% of the account. A POSITIVE leftover is now cash: it is money the broker's total includes but its holdings do not account for — settlement cash, a dividend just received, a pending trade — and calling it cash is nearly always true, while calling it "more CDs" is a claim about what the person OWNS that we cannot support. A NEGATIVE leftover (priced holdings exceeding the stated total) stays absorbed by the largest class, because it is a pricing artifact rather than money and writing it into cash would show a negative cash balance. Totals still reconcile exactly either way.
rows.why: Founder question 2026-08-11: "why is cash added to CD and not cash?" — asked while checking the $500 difference on the Vanguard account page.

rows.his_words: $500 is what I added manually as a deposit to the Vanguard account. It never asked me if it was in cash or something else?
rows.plain: A deposit only moves money into an account’s cash if that account HAS a cash figure to move it into. His Vanguard account lists its holdings individually and had no cash figure, so a $500 deposit vanished from the balance. The fix is at the root — the account now has somewhere for cash to land.
rows.means: THE ROOT CAUSE BEHIND THE $500. A deposit only moves money into an account's cash sleeve when that account HAS one (derive_balance set, or a cash figure already present). The founder's Vanguard account itemises its holdings but its broker never sent a cash figure, so the deposit simply inflated the stated total — the holdings could no longer explain it, and the unexplained difference was then inferred elsewhere. That is the whole chain behind $500 of deposited money being counted as more CDs. Now: money arriving in an account that itemises holdings OPENS the cash sleeve and lands there, and the stated total rises by the same amount, so the classification explains the whole figure with nothing left to infer. A plain account with nothing to itemise is unchanged — it just grows, and no sleeve is invented. AND THE SCREEN SAYS SO: the deposit sheet now reads "Lands as cash in this account. When you invest it, record the purchase and it moves into that holding" (withdrawals get the matching sentence). It never needed to ASK — money arriving at a broker IS settlement cash until a purchase moves it — but it did need to say.

rows.his_words: pressed sync now... the message says Updated. Anything still listed here needs a re-login. Not sure what got updated, both accounts still listed to sync. Also no place to re-login.
rows.plain: Three fixes behind one thing he reported. The worst: the sheet ignored what the sync actually returned and always said “Updated” — so when nothing had refreshed it claimed success while the rows sat unchanged. A message that lies by omission is worse than no message.
rows.means: THREE FIXES BEHIND ONE FOUNDER REPORT. (a) THE MESSAGE LIED BY OMISSION: the sheet ignored what the sync returned and always said "Updated", so when nothing was refreshed it claimed success while both rows sat exactly where they were. It now reports the actual count — "Updated 2 accounts" — or, at zero, "Nothing could be refreshed — your broker didn't answer. That usually means the connection has expired: use Reconnect below." (b) THERE WAS NOWHERE TO RE-LOGIN: the sheet told people a re-login was needed while offering only a Sync button. Every connection row now carries a second door, Reconnect, exactly as the approved State F mock drew it ("Sync now › Reconnect ›") — a sync can never revive a connection the provider has dropped. (c) THE ROOT CAUSE OF THE SILENCE: when the provider reports NO connections while the app still holds accounts marked connected (a revoked link, an expired session, or a provider-side user reset — the founder ran a SnapTrade purge on 2026-08-04), nothing threw, so nothing was recorded and those accounts just aged quietly. Every such account is now recorded as unreachable, so it SAYS it cannot be refreshed and offers the re-login.

rows.his_words: when I click add your age it takes me to plan main screen, and 1 answer left takes me to sharpen your plan. Does not seem like optimal flow.
rows.plain: A line that names a missing answer now takes you to THAT answer. “Add your age and it becomes yours” went to the Plan screen, whose own “1 answer left” went somewhere else again — two taps, and still not the field you were asked for.
rows.means: A LINE THAT NAMES AN ANSWER NOW LANDS ON THAT ANSWER. "Add your age and it becomes yours" went to the Plan HUB, whose own "1 answer left" went to Sharpen your plan — a SEVEN-item completeness checklist driven by a different engine than the three-answer count. Three hops to answer one question, and the last one did not ask it. Worse, the app had NO screen that captured your age at all: the only writer was the What-if slider, which is why the line had nowhere sensible to go. NEW /plan-answers asks exactly the answers the odds are missing (your age · what you spend · what you have), each saving as you type, with ?focus= opening straight at one; it shows THE ODDS on the same screen the moment all three are in, so nobody has to travel to find out whether it worked. Net worth's sample line and the Plan hub's door both point here now. Sharpen keeps its own job — how complete is the whole plan — and stops being the destination for "see your real odds", which is a different question. The three ways in (connect · import · by hand) moved to ONE shared list so two screens cannot word them differently. Route whitelisted in the guard (the T22 class), and the dead-route guard covers it.

rows.his_words: for calculating assets to count towards retirement - it should be all assets minus primary home and primary car. If they want they can change which asset should not count.
rows.plain: HIS RULE: everything you own counts toward retirement EXCEPT your primary home and your primary car. So cash counts, because it is money you can spend; a rental counts, because you can sell it; and a SECOND car counts. Only the home you live in and the car you drive are excluded.
rows.means: FOUNDER RULE: everything you own counts toward retirement EXCEPT your primary home and your primary car. Cash now counts (it is money you can spend), a rental counts (you can sell it), and a SECOND car counts — only the roof over your head and the car you drive are assumed off the table, because selling those is not a retirement plan. A 529 stays out (legally someone else's). The primary car = the most valuable vehicle, so a two-car household keeps the second as a real asset. Any of it is changeable per account, and the person's own choice always beats the default. This SUPERSEDES the old Term #7 default (property 0%, cash 0%, investments 100%) — five pinned tests were carrying that rule and each was updated with the reason. Knock-on, stated honestly: the expected-growth blend now includes cash, so a cash-heavy pot shows a LOWER growth rate — correct, because such a pot really does grow more slowly.

rows.raw:
FOUNDER RULE: everything you own counts toward retirement EXCEPT your primary home and your primary car. Cash now counts (it is money you can spend), a rental counts (you can sell it), and a SECOND car counts — only the roof over your head and the car you drive are assumed off the table, because selling those is not a retirement plan. A 529 stays out (legally someone else's). The primary car = the most valuable vehicle, so a two-car household keeps the second as a real asset. Any of it is changeable per account, and the person's own choice always beats the default. This SUPERSEDES the old Term #7 default (property 0%, cash 0%, investments 100%) — five pinned tests were carrying that rule and each was updated with the reason. Knock-on, stated honestly: the expected-growth blend now includes cash, so a cash-heavy pot shows a LOWER growth rate — correct, because such a pot really does grow more slowly.

rows.his_words: On home and NW screen - if all the information is available - what happens?
rows.plain: Once all three answers exist, Net worth shows the real verdict sentence with its numbers and tapping the card opens the Plan screen — rather than continuing to ask for something already given.
rows.means: WHEN ALL THREE ANSWERS EXIST: Net worth shows the real verdict sentence ("Uncertain — retire at 65 with ~$1,607,000, lasting past 90 with ~$2,402,000 to spare ›") and tapping the card opens the Plan tab; Home shows the real gauge and percentage with "See the full picture ›", also to Plan. No sample appears beside a real verdict, and the bare "See your plan ›" appears nowhere. Verified by rendering both screens with a complete profile. THE HOLE THAT QUESTION EXPOSED: planDoor counted ANY account with a balance as "what you have", while the odds run on what is EARMARKED for retirement — so someone whose only asset is the home they live in looked COMPLETE to the door and produced no odds at all, landing on exactly the bare fallback we removed everywhere else. The gate now means what the odds mean (earmarked > 0), and owning things while none of them count is reported as its own case — "choose what counts toward retirement" — which lands on the answers screen where the home can be ticked in. The door also credits what actually counts rather than every balance on file.

rows.his_words: Uncertain — retire at 65 with ~$1,607,000, lasting past 90 with ~$2,402,000 to spare — what does uncertain mean?
rows.plain: A verdict word must carry its number. Net worth was the only screen showing the word alone — Home said “78% odds of lasting to age 90” and the Plan screen said “84 in 100 paths”, while Net worth said just “Uncertain”, which tells you nothing you can act on.
rows.means: A BARE ADJECTIVE IS NOT A VERDICT. Net worth was the ONLY surface showing the verdict word with no number beside it — Home says "78% odds of lasting to age 90", the Plan hub says "84 in 100 paths", Net worth said just "Uncertain". The number travels with the word now: "Uncertain — 78 in 100 · retire at 65 with ~$1,607,000, lasting past 90 with ~$2,402,000 to spare ›". AND THE DEEPER CONFUSION IS ANSWERED WHERE IT IS ASKED: the info dot already on that card now defines the three words by their bands (Likely 80+, Uncertain 60-79, Unlikely under 60; retired: Holding / Watch closely / Running short) and explains why a plan can read "Uncertain" while showing money to spare — the dollar figure is the MIDDLE of the 500 runs, the odds count how many lasted at all, so "78 in 100 with $2.4m to spare" means a typical run finishes rich and 22 runs in 100 still ran out. Two true facts, not a mistake; averages hide exactly that, which is why the odds exist.

They were built only from itemised holding rows, so an account with a balance and no holdings — a CD account, anything hand-entered — vanished from the list, and the per-account walks silently stopped summing to the all-accounts walk above them. STILL OPEN, listed for the founder: category rows are not yet tappable through to a category-detail screen; the handoff's per-category "/yr" treatment for bonds and cash (their stated yield rather than a window return); the account page's "you entered this" tag with an edit affordance on user-entered records and its "See all activity (older than X)" door. NOT ADOPTED, per the founder's instruction to take UX and not calculations: the handoff's own figures and its category-return definitions — ours stay.

rows.plain: Every row in the activity list says where it came from. The list mixed the broker’s own records with rows you typed and showed them identically — so a $500 deposit mistyped as $5,000 was indistinguishable from the broker’s own figure.
rows.means: EVERY ACTIVITY ROW NOW SAYS WHERE IT CAME FROM. The list mixed the broker's own records with rows the person typed and showed them identically — so a $500 deposit typed as $5,000 was indistinguishable from a Vanguard record, and equally unfixable. Your rows wear "you entered this" and a pencil; broker rows read "from Vanguard" and offer nothing, because the next sync would overwrite any change. CORRECTING a row goes through the ONE transactions engine as a reversal plus a fresh record, so the balance moves by the same tested rules as every other change rather than being patched behind the ledger's back; a row the ledger cannot reverse says so plainly and offers a correcting entry instead. Delete is on the same sheet. NOTE: the handoff's other activity item — "See all activity (older than Jul 19)" — was already built in a different form: the page shows the newest eight and offers "See all activity (N) ›". Ours truncates by count rather than by window, which after the newest-first fix is the clearer of the two.

rows.raw:
EVERY ACTIVITY ROW NOW SAYS WHERE IT CAME FROM. The list mixed the broker's own records with rows the person typed and showed them identically — so a $500 deposit typed as $5,000 was indistinguishable from a Vanguard record, and equally unfixable. Your rows wear "you entered this" and a pencil; broker rows read "from Vanguard" and offer nothing, because the next sync would overwrite any change. CORRECTING a row goes through the ONE transactions engine as a reversal plus a fresh record, so the balance moves by the same tested rules as every other change rather than being patched behind the ledger's back; a row the ledger cannot reverse says so plainly and offers a correcting entry instead. Delete is on the same sheet. NOTE: the handoff's other activity item — "See all activity (older than Jul 19)" — was already built in a different form: the page shows the newest eight and offers "See all activity (N) ›". Ours truncates by count rather than by window, which after the newest-first fix is the clearer of the two.

rows.his_words: combine plan answers and Try what-ifs into one screen… add a big one-time cost… reverse calculate the monthly/annual savings goal based on targeted retirement nest egg
rows.plain: He settled the structure of the Plan screen himself rather than having it explored again: the tab is TWO sections — your retirement plan, and the decisions. The brief was rewritten to say so, and the earlier version kept but superseded.
rows.means: FOUNDER SETTLED THE PLAN ARCHITECTURE; brief bumped to mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/PLAN-REDESIGN-BRIEF-v2-2026-08-12.md (v1 kept, superseded). DECIDED: (1) the Plan tab is TWO sections — "Your retirement plan" and "Decisions you can make today" — with "When can I retire?" in section 1, because it is the retire-at input wearing a question mark. (2) Section 1 is ONE MERGED SCREEN: the three answer questions + the What-if sandbox + the read-only drivers + the big-one-time-costs list, every field prefilled from a default or a calculation, anything genuinely unknown LABELLED as missing with a way to add it. Retire-at default 65 and plan-to default 90 become VISIBLE and changeable (they are already the code defaults but were applied silently). Retirement spending gets ASKED plainly, prefilled from today's spending — the app currently derives it and then tells the person "you set it", which is not true. (3) NEW RULE — facts save, choices commit: age/spending/what-counts/big-costs save on the spot; retire-at, claim age and extra saving stay drafts until "Use as my plan". (4) The outcome is two figures plus a line: the odds sentence, a goal tracker against a TARGET NEST EGG, and the yearly saving needed. The target is COMPUTED (the pile that puts the odds at 80%, the Likely boundary), not typed — a typed number stays as an optional marked override — so the tracker and the gauge are one fact drawn twice and can never contradict each other. The required saving is shown against the tax-advantaged room the app already knows. (5) The IMPOSSIBLE-REQUIRED-SAVING state is a required design: when the honest number exceeds what the person earns, say it plainly then pivot to the three levers that move (retire later, spend less, claim later) — never "you have failed". (6) The outcome must stay visible on a long screen. (7) What-if is absorbed and deleted; Multi-goal, Roth, Social Security timing, required withdrawals and the stress test survive in section 2, each row earning its place by saying what it is worth in dollars or points.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-12, across three exchanges: the six retirement inputs + defaults 65/90; the two-section layout; then "combine plan answers and Try what-ifs into one screen… add a big one-time cost… reverse calculate the monthly/annual savings goal based on targeted retirement nest egg" — with my recommendation to DERIVE the target from the odds rather than take a typed number, accepted.

rows.his_words: s not say Uncertain — 60% odds of lasting to age 90. uncertain and giving it 60% probability does not make sense. it should be either or. Let
rows.plain: The verdict word is removed. The odds now read “60% odds of lasting to age 90” with nothing in front of it — no “Likely”, no “Uncertain”. Removed on all seven screens that showed it, so no screen keeps a word the others have dropped.
rows.means: THE WORD IS GONE. The odds now read "60% odds of lasting to age 90" with nothing in front. Removed on all seven surfaces that showed it — Home, Net worth, Plan hub, Plan answers, Will it last, Cash flow, Multi-goal — plus the desktop sandbox and the spoken screen-reader labels. BOTH rival word-sets are deleted from the code (Likely/Uncertain/Unlikely and the retiree Holding/Watch closely/Running short), which also closes the inconsistency where one retiree at 100% read "Holding" on the Plan tab and "Likely" on Will-it-last. The Multi-goal row that read "Uncertain to Uncertain" is gone — the row above it already says 60% to 67%. The info dot no longer defines a word that does not exist: it now opens WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS and says plainly why no word sits beside the percentage. Tests rewritten to pin the ABSENCE of the words on every surface, and the cross-screen agreement pin now reads the accessibility labels (what a screen reader hears) instead of hunting for a word beside a number — a stronger pin, because it fails if a screen shows the number without saying what it is. Gates: 1565 tests green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-12: "let's not say Uncertain — 60% odds of lasting to age 90. uncertain and giving it 60% probability does not make sense. it should be either or. Let's remove uncertain." Applied to all three bands and both voices, not just the middle word — the same objection holds for "Likely — 85%", and keeping one word while dropping another would have been worse than either.

rows.his_words: add $38,000/yr for 7 years to reach your target and raise your odds to 80%
rows.plain: The designer’s Plan handoff arrived and was reviewed against the code rather than accepted on sight. What was adopted as drawn is recorded, and so is what was not.
rows.means: HANDOFF IN (Plan-requirements.md + Plan.dc.html), reviewed against the code; review saved at mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/HANDOFF-REVIEW-2026-08-12.md. ADOPTED as drawn: the two-gauge hero (odds left, assets-vs-target right, both dollar figures beneath, then the bridge sentence "add $38,000/yr for 7 years to reach your target and raise your odds to 80%"), FACT/DRAFT chips as the at-a-glance tell between a saved fact and a draft choice, all five states of the merged screen with a pinned outcome strip, the honest impossible-saving state with three levers, worth-labelled Section 2 rows, and the retiree paycheck variant in place of a target gauge. FIVE CORRECTIONS before code: (1) BLOCKING — the design puts the verdict word on every screen ("Uncertain — 60% odds…"); the founder deleted the word hours after the brief went out, so every such line loses its word and nothing else moves. Not the designer's error: brief v2 asked them to pick a word-set; the sequencing was mine. (2) The handoff calls the 31-87% range a confidence band on the estimate and forbids saying "your odds could be as low as 31%" — but our engine derives that band by re-running the whole simulation at 2 percentage points lower and higher assumed return, so it IS a market-outcome range; the shipped wording "across bad-to-good markets" is correct and theirs would be false. (3) It puts the home's 4.5% growth into the blended return of a portfolio that excludes the home. (4) June's "spend more" row says "+$1,600/mo room" where the handoff's own arithmetic gives $2,555 unused safe draw — $1,600 is what she IS using. (5) The empty-state sample shows 74%; the app's sample is 84%, used everywhere. NEW ENGINE WORK identified (does not exist today): the derived target solved backwards for 80% odds, the required annual saving, per-lever point deltas, goals/debt wired into the odds engine for Section 2 labels, and the draft-vs-committed state layer — with a performance risk when one stepper move triggers a target solve plus a saving solve plus three lever runs. OPEN QUESTION for the founder: the handoff puts the merged screen behind a link from the tab rather than inside it, so the tab is a summary and the inputs are one tap away — that decides whether a person can change their retire age without leaving the tab.

HANDOFF IN (Plan-requirements.md + Plan.dc.html), reviewed against the code; review saved at mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/HANDOFF-REVIEW-2026-08-12.md. ADOPTED as drawn: the two-gauge hero (odds left, assets-vs-target right, both dollar figures beneath, then the bridge sentence "add $38,000/yr for 7 years to reach your target and raise your odds to 80%"), FACT/DRAFT chips as the at-a-glance tell between a saved fact and a draft choice, all five states of the merged screen with a pinned outcome strip, the honest impossible-saving state with three levers, worth-labelled Section 2 rows, and the retiree paycheck variant in place of a target gauge. FIVE CORRECTIONS before code: (1) BLOCKING — the design puts the verdict word on every screen ("Uncertain — 60% odds…"); the founder deleted the word hours after the brief went out, so every such line loses its word and nothing else moves. Not the designer's error: brief v2 asked them to pick a word-set; the sequencing was mine. (2) The handoff calls the 31-87% range a confidence band on the estimate and forbids saying "your odds could be as low as 31%" — but our engine derives that band by re-running the whole simulation at 2 percentage points lower and higher assumed return, so it IS a market-outcome range; the shipped wording "across bad-to-good markets" is correct and theirs would be false. (3) It puts the home's 4.5% growth into the blended return of a portfolio that excludes the home. (4) June's "spend more" row says "+$1,600/mo room" where the handoff's own arithmetic gives $2,555 unused safe draw — $1,600 is what she IS using. (5) The empty-state sample shows 74%; the app's sample is 84%, used everywhere. NEW ENGINE WORK identified (does not exist today): the derived target solved backwards for 80% odds, the required annual saving, per-lever point deltas, goals/debt wired into the odds engine for Section 2 labels, and the draft-vs-committed state layer — with a performance risk when one stepper move triggers a target solve plus a saving solve plus three lever runs. OPEN QUESTION for the founder: the handoff puts the merged screen behind a link from the tab rather than inside it, so the tab is a summary and the inputs are one tap away — that decides whether a person can change their retire age without leaving the tab.

rows.his_words: I am on with $
rows.plain: Building the calculation removed the need for the second dial. The target is now worked out backwards — the app finds the pot you would need on your first day of retirement to reach 80% odds — so one score plus arithmetic says everything two dials were saying.
rows.means: BUILDING THE ENGINE KILLED THE SECOND GAUGE. src/domain/planning/target.ts solves the odds backwards: targetAtRetirement (the pot on day one of retirement that reaches 80% odds, by bisection on the same 400-path simulation), requiredAnnualSaving (a second solve on the real plan, returned as the EXTRA over what they already save), and leverDeltas (each lever a genuine re-run with one change; claiming later raises the CHECK by 8%/yr, and the lever is hidden entirely when there is no Social Security on file). 11 engine tests incl. a speed budget — the whole outcome block is 238ms. THE FINDING: run a struggling person through it and the design contradicts itself — 31% odds beside a target gauge reading 80% of the way. Deriving the target does NOT prevent this, because progress compares ONE future (the median) against a threshold while the odds count how many of 400 futures lasted; the spread is what separates them. Founder accepted the fix: the right-hand side stops being a rival percentage. Asked whether it should be a gauge, a bar or text, the answer is TEXT — any proportional shape IS a score, and the eye believes the shape even after the number is removed. So: ONE score (the odds gauge), then three money lines that subtract to each other — On track for / Target nest egg (founder's words, replacing "You'd need") / Short — with the shortfall bold, then the bridge sentence naming the yearly amount and how much fits in tax-advantaged room. Above 100% the third line flips to "More than you need", which a gauge could not have drawn. The impossible state says the honest number once and turns to the levers. Built as src/components/PlanOutcome.tsx with 7 tests (one-score pin, the arithmetic ties to the dollar, the ahead state, the bridge, the impossible state, hide-balances, and the nothing-computable state). Mock deviation logged: the handoff's illustrative 60% / $1.9M / $38,000 do not survive contact with the engine — Pat as specified is 81% with a $1.14M target.

rows.his_words: inputs on the tab.
rows.plain: His ruling, “inputs on the tab”: the first section IS the Plan tab, not a link to another screen. The tab reads: your retirement plan, then the outcome, then what you are on track for, your target and the shortfall.
rows.means: SECTION 1 IS THE TAB, not a link behind it (founder ruling: "inputs on the tab"). The Plan tab now reads: YOUR RETIREMENT PLAN band → the outcome (one score, then On track for / Target nest egg / Short, then the bridge sentence) → FACTS — SAVE AS YOU GO (age, monthly spending in retirement, what counts, big one-time costs) → CHOICES — TRY THEM, NOTHING CHANGES YET (retire at, plan to age, extra saving) → DECISIONS YOU CAN MAKE TODAY. The draft layer lives at the tab so a stepper moves the number above it live (walked: 55% → 62% on one press of Retire at, with the projection and target moving too); "Use as my plan" confirms and writes. FOUR DEFECTS FOUND BY WALKING THE BUILT SCREEN, all fixed before reporting: (1) the outcome printed "More than you need $74,845" beside "Adding $43,000 a year closes it" — the median can clear the target while the odds do not, so the gap line now stands down whenever its sign disagrees with the odds and the bridge speaks alone; (2) the old narrative pair ("You could retire at 65 with…" + "…if you retire at 65, and spend $5,200/mo — your planned spending, you set it") was deleted: it repeated what the block above now says, did not follow the draft, and claimed "you set it" of a figure the app had derived; (3) the "Try what-ifs — a sandbox" door removed — the steppers ARE the sandbox, sitting under the number they move, so four sandboxes became one; (4) "When can I retire?" and "What big costs are coming?" removed from the decision list — both now live in section 1, and three copies of one question is how it got confusing. rows.his_words: Target nest egg is a number entered by the user based on what is their target
rows.plain:
Two rulings about the target nest egg:
1. It is a figure YOU type, marked as yours — “What’s your target nest egg?” — not one the app derives and presents as fact.
2. The app’s own 80%-odds figure becomes the suggestion you can accept, rather than the answer.
rows.means: TWO RULINGS. (1) THE TARGET IS TYPED, NOT DERIVED. It is 'Your target nest egg' / 'What's your target nest egg?' — a fact the person enters, marked as theirs. The app's own 80%-odds figure becomes the SUGGESTION offered when the field is left blank, never the headline. This reverses brief v2 §'The target is computed, not typed', which was my call, not the founder's. Consequence: the money block reads down to THEIR gap (target − on track for = short) and the saving sentence closes THAT gap; the odds stay a separate honest number, because a pile of money and the chance it survives being spent are different things. (2) THE RETIREMENT PARAMETERS ARE QUESTIONS, NOT LABELS — current age, target retirement age, plan-to age, nest egg / retirement assets: 'How old are you?', 'When do you want to retire?', 'How long should the money last?', 'What counts toward retirement?', 'What big one-time costs are coming?', 'How much extra can you save each month?'. Founder: 'These are simple to understand.' The same words must land on all FOUR surfaces that ask them (Plan tab · Retirement cockpit · What drives this? · What if I save more?) or the screens will disagree. MOCK FIRST: mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/plan-questions-and-typed-target-v1-2026-08-12.html (rich state + first day + a before/after wording table). NOT BUILT — awaiting the founder's yes.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-12, answering my audit finding D1: 'Target nest egg is a number entered by the user based on what is their target' + 'you type it and call it Your target nest egg... We should not have these retirement parameters as simply parameters versus framing it as a question.' The audit had held the target to a definition the founder never chose.

rows.his_words: t you create instruction for claude design to design it. too much information on one screen
rows.plain: His verdict on the built screen: “too much information on one screen” and “the way you designed it is very confusing.” It goes back to design — and the structure is settled BY HIM rather than explored again, because exploring it again is what produced the confusion.
rows.means: FOUNDER VERDICT ON THE BUILT SCREEN: 'too much information on one screen' + 'the way you designed it is very confusing' → back to design, with the structure settled by him rather than explored again. THE STRUCTURE: (1) TWO DIALS — odds on the left, assets-vs-target on the right — and one sentence beneath: '$909,152 of $2,000,000 target — short $1,090,848'. The right dial compares what they have TODAY to their typed target (45%), NOT the projected-at-retirement figure; the $653,237 shortfall from an earlier draft is wrong for this design and is called out as such. (2) 'YOUR PLAN AT A GLANCE', COLLAPSED BY DEFAULT: seven rows at ONE level of hierarchy — age · target retirement age · plan-to age · monthly spending in retirement · target nest egg · current retirement assets (expandable + editable) · big one-time costs. Anything beneath a row (an account, a cost) is one level down and must be drawn as one level down. Every row is a QUESTION. (3) DECISIONS YOU CAN MAKE TODAY = pay off the mortgage early · convert to a Roth · when to claim Social Security AT 60+ ONLY — each shown only when it applies to that person. The Social Security row ANSWERS ITSELF IN PLACE ('waiting from 67 to 70 pays $624 more a month: $3,224 against $2,600') instead of routing to another screen. CORRECTION LOGGED: the founder said '67 or 72'; the delayed credit STOPS AT 70, so 72 would promise money that does not exist — the brief specifies 62/67/70. (4) RETIREE: the paycheck replaces the target dial. (5) The Social Security claim-window card is no longer a 'next decision' for someone in their 50s. Brief: mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/PLAN-REDESIGN-BRIEF-v3-2026-08-12.md (v1, v2 kept). Three questions left open for the designer to propose on: the dropped 'extra saving each month' stepper, save-immediately vs draft-and-commit now that all seven sit in one panel, and whether the dated card survives at all.

rows.his_words: When person click on Pay off the mortgage early -> where does it go?
rows.plain: Where each decision row leads, settled: converting to a Roth opens the existing Roth screen, which is not to be redesigned; when to claim Social Security is answered in the row itself and goes nowhere; and paying off the mortgage early moves to Cash flow, where the debt is.
rows.means: WHERE EACH DECISION ROW GOES, SETTLED: 'Convert to a Roth' → the EXISTING Roth screen (built; not to be redesigned); 'When to claim Social Security' → nowhere, answers in the row; 'Pay off the mortgage early' → nowhere, opens IN PLACE with a live control. THE MORTGAGE ROW IS NOT A FACT TO READ, IT IS A THING TO DO: a stepper for the extra monthly payment, payoff date and interest saved moving as it changes, and a commit that makes the payment part of the plan and shows it in Cash flow as real money out. It must show BOTH SIDES — 'clears Nov 2045 instead of Oct 2054, saving $143,300 in interest' AND '$500 a month not invested takes your odds from 48% to 43%' — because interest-saved alone always reads as an obvious win and at a mortgage rate near the assumed return it is close to a wash. WHAT THIS COSTS, FOUND BY CHECKING THE ENGINE: the retirement simulation HAS NO CONCEPT OF DEBT AT ALL (zero mentions in simulate() or willItLast). Three builds required: (a) store the extra payment — today it is an unsaved useState text box on the Cash flow Debts tab that forgets on exit; (b) contributions must become a SCHEDULE, not one flat annual number, so $6,000/yr less goes in while the mortgage runs and the whole payment frees up when it clears; (c) the simulation must know a payment ENDS. DEFECT SURFACED BY (c), PRE-EXISTING AND UNRELATED TO THIS ROW: retirement spending is charged flat + inflation for every year of the plan, so if a person included their mortgage in that figure the app keeps charging it after the house is paid off — Pat's mortgage clears 2054, Pat's plan runs to 2058, four years of a payment that will not exist. TODAY'S ODDS ARE PESSIMISTIC for anyone whose mortgage ends inside their plan, and no screen says so. Logged in brief v3 §6 as engine work, flagged to the designer as not-yet-available.

The question exposed that brief v3 named three decision rows and said where only one of them led — my omission, closed the same hour.

rows.his_words: Is a Roth move worth it?
rows.plain: One rule for a decision row: it ANSWERS IN PLACE unless the decision needs more than one thing set. Paying off the mortgage early and when to claim Social Security are answered in the row; anything needing several inputs opens its own screen.
rows.means: ONE RULE FOR DECISION ROWS: a row ANSWERS IN PLACE unless the decision needs more than one thing set. In place: pay off the mortgage early (live stepper + commit) · when to claim Social Security (60+) · can I spend more? (live stepper) · have you taken your required withdrawal? (confirm without leaving, year-by-year one tap away). Own screen: WHICH ACCOUNT DO I DRAW FROM FIRST (new — today the row dumps the person on the whole Cash flow tab; the new screen carries the order, the reason per account, the tax cost and the steering) · IS CONVERTING TO A ROTH WORTH IT (renamed from 'Is a Roth move worth it?'; keeps the EXISTING Roth screen, not to be redesigned; carries $420,000 pre-tax as its worth). ODDS ARE AN OUTPUT — founder: 'Instead of artificially changing odds, let's look to get the numbers right. Odds are output and we should not modify it.' No adjustment, no penalty, ever: model the money honestly, run it twice, print both results. Consequence — the mortgage fix is not an odds hack but a MODELLING fix: when a debt outlives the retirement date the plan shows an explicit editable line 'Mortgage payment $2,400/mo until 2054', auto-filled from the loan, and the simulation charges it until that year and stops. That also closes the pre-existing pessimism (flat retirement spending charged forever, so a paid-off mortgage keeps being charged). PAYING IN FULL: the app never moves money and never asks which account to debit — it states that once paid we capture it from the connected bank or an uploaded statement, the person marks the mortgage paid off, and net worth updates everywhere from that one act. CAN I SPEND MORE: wording is the founder's verbatim — 'estimated amount you can draw more every month' — and no new engine is needed (it is the same solve that already produces the retiree's monthly draw, minus what they already spend). THE ODDS FLOOR IS THE PERSON'S SETTING, default 80%, ONE setting used everywhere the app answers a how-much question, shown wherever a number depends on it. *** THE WORD 'SAFE' IS BANNED ON ANYTHING TO DO WITH MONEY *** — founder: 'we should never call anything safe as we don't know. Always ensure legally we are not saying anything binding.' A legal position, not a style preference. Founder-chosen replacements: Safe to spend → LEFT TO SPEND · Safe draw from savings → DRAW FROM SAVINGS · within the safe range → within the ~4% guideline · Your safety net → YOUR CUSHION. MEASURED SCOPE: 29 user-visible occurrences across 14 files (Home, Cash flow, Plan, PaycheckCard, MonthDetail, PaycheckMonths, RetirementCockpit, DrawSteerSheet, Tips, MonthlyIncome, glossary, paycheck engine, lens). 'Safe to spend' is a HEADLINE label on Cash flow, not a footnote — this sweeps as ONE change or not at all. Out of scope: non-money uses ('your data is safe', 'saved it somewhere safe'). SWEEP NOT YET DONE — awaiting the word.

rows.his_words: s the order in which these appear on screen? And how we are determining that order?
rows.plain: His question — “what’s the order and how are we determining it?” — found that there was NO rule. The decision rows were written one after another in whatever order they happened to sit in the file. They now have an ordering rule.
rows.means: FOUND BY THE FOUNDER'S QUESTION 'what's the order and how are we determining it?': there was NO rule. The rows are hard-coded JSX in PlanHubScreen, one after another, in whatever order the lines happen to sit in the file — no sort, no rank. The only ordering principle anywhere in the app governs a single card (nextDecision(): 'a required withdrawal due this year outranks everything — it has a deadline'). Brief v3 had simply carried the order the founder typed them in, which was the same gap in a different place. NOW SETTLED: (1) ANYTHING DATED GOES FIRST, because it expires — extends the existing deadline principle from one card to the whole list. (2) EVERYTHING ELSE HOLDS A FIXED ORDER PER LENS, chosen by what is most on the mind at that stage of life, and it does NOT re-sort as balances move — a person who learns where a row sits finds it there next month. Working: Social Security (60+) · pay off the mortgage early · is converting to a Roth worth it. Drawing down: Social Security (only if not yet claiming) · can I spend more · which account do I draw from first · pay off the mortgage early · is converting to a Roth worth it. REJECTED, with the reason recorded: ranking by size or by impact, because rows would change position between visits with the person having done nothing — and because the mortgage row has no points figure until the engine work lands. (3) A row only takes a position IF IT APPLIES — the founder's own test: 'if I don't have mortgage will mortgage appear for me? if I don't have 401K, conversion of Roth is meaningless.' No: absent, never greyed out, never 'no mortgage on file'. Expect a SHORT list — Pat at 58 sees two rows, June at 72 sees three. FLAGGED AS MINE not his, for confirmation: Social Security at the top of both columns, and the mortgage row appearing for retirees at all. TO BUILD: this is a rule the code applies, never again a sequence someone types.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-12: 'what's the order in which these appear on screen? And how we are determining that order?' then chose deadlines-first + relevance, and defined relevance by his own two examples (no mortgage, no 401k) which are about PRESENCE; the tie-break among rows that do appear was settled separately as stage-of-life.

rows.his_words: round up
rows.plain: His ruling: “round up”. Both the target and the shortfall are found by hunting for the smallest amount that clears 80% odds, then rounded UP so they read like human numbers — and rounding up means the promise the screen makes is true rather than nearly true.
rows.means: Founder ruling: 'round up'. ONE CAUSE, TWO SYMPTOMS, one word each. Both figures are found by hunting for the smallest amount that clears 80% odds, then rounded to read like human numbers — and both rounded to the NEAREST step, which can land back BELOW the line the search had just cleared. targetAtRetirement: Math.round(found/10_000) → Math.ceil. requiredAnnualSaving: Math.round(found/500) → Math.ceil. MEASURED BEFORE/AFTER on Pat: suggested target $1,370,000 delivering 76% → $1,380,000 delivering 81%; required saving $53,000 delivering 79% → $53,500 delivering 81%. Erring high was the deliberate choice — the sentence on screen says 'this gets you to 80%' and it must be true; the alternative (the exact solved figure, $1,374,382) is precise and unreadable as a target. NEW PIN src/domain/planning/target_rounding.test.ts holds the PROMISE not the implementation: holding the target must deliver ≥80%, saving the figure must deliver ≥80%, both must round to a whole step, and ONE STEP LOWER MUST MISS — so the fix cannot be gamed by simply inflating the numbers. Gates: 1618 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. D1's original defect (the target is not the number that gives 80%) was already mostly settled by the typed-target ruling; this closes the residue — the SUGGESTION we offer when the field is left blank.

rows.his_words: good with recommendation
rows.plain: Two things fixed with his agreement. The most useful line on the screen had disappeared — the design ended the section without it — and it comes back, because the line that tells you what to do next is the one you came for.
rows.means: Founder: 'good with recommendation'. The suppression rule behind D4 dies with the typed target. TWO THINGS IT LEFT: (1) THE MOST ACTIONABLE LINE ON THE SCREEN HAD VANISHED. The v3 handoff ends the hero at 'short $1,090,848' and goes straight to the glance — stating a problem, offering nothing. Restored to brief §3.1, now measured against THEIR target: 'Saving $84,500 a year over your 7 years to 65 reaches your target.' CRITICAL METHOD NOTE: it must be SOLVED, not formula'd. The obvious closed-form annuity calculation gives $82,000 for Pat and lands at $1,977,544 — $22,000 short of the target it just promised to reach, which is exactly the D1/D2 defect class in a new place. Measured properly by search: $84,500 lands at $2,021,514, one $500 step lower lands at $1,994,407 and misses. Added to §6 as engine work (today's solve targets 80% ODDS, a different question) and it carries the same pin shape as D1/D2. (2) NEW REQUIRED STATE 6 in brief §5: ALREADY PAST YOUR OWN TARGET, drawn nowhere. Not a rare case — type $800,000 and Pat is at 114% of target with 45% odds: a dial pegged past full beside a number under half. Not a contradiction, two honest answers to two different questions, and the screen must carry it without either looking like an error. Mirror case specified too: a $1,500,000 target is reached by saving $24,000/yr at 64% odds — you can hit your number exactly and still not be at 80%. Both go to Claude Design in the next pass.

rows.plain: His instruction: “fix it”. The retirement paycheck showed two bare amounts with NO NAMES beside them — a bill with the line items blanked out — directly above a note saying it was the same paycheck as Home. Each amount now says whose money it is.
rows.means: Founder: 'fix it'. June's paycheck on the Plan tab rendered two bare amounts with NO NAMES beside them — a bill with the line items blanked out — directly above a note reading 'the same paycheck as Home's card, one engine, one set of numbers'. Cause: PlanHubScreen read g.label off each guaranteed-income row; the engine's field is g.source. Home's PaycheckCard, MonthDetailScreen and PaycheckMonthsScreen all read it correctly — the Plan tab was the ONLY one of four consumers that was wrong, so the class needed no sweep. One word. NEW PIN src/__tests__/paycheck_row_names.test.tsx: (1) the Plan tab names every guaranteed row, (2) it names them the same way Home does, rendered through the one shared engine, (3) a source GUARD so no screen reaches for .label on a guaranteed row again. THE PIN WAS VERIFIED TO BITE — the fix was reverted, 2 of the 3 tests failed, and it was restored (the Home comparison passes either way, correctly, since Home was never broken). Fixed in place rather than left for the redesign: a one-word change, and a nameless paycheck is exactly what a device walk would hit first. Gates: 1621 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: who is that someone
rows.plain: His decision: “if the odds are zero — don’t show zero.” Zero never appears anywhere. In its place, in the order he approved: an honest sentence first, then the routes that cost nothing, then paid advice.
rows.means: Founder 2026-08-13 (audit D6): 'if the odds are zero — don't show zero', then option ONE — THE ZERO NEVER APPEARS ANYWHERE. Order approved: honest sentence FIRST, free routes SECOND, fee-only hourly planner THIRD. SCOPE IS FOUR SURFACES: oddsLine() is one shared helper printed by Plan, Home, Net worth and the spoken screen-reader label (the founder's own 2026-08-11 one-wording rule), so a Plan-only change would leave Home greeting the person with a bare 0%. WHAT MEASURING IT CHANGED — the original finding was 'the levers list can come back empty'; the real story is that OUR LEVERS ARE TOO TIMID. They test retiring 2 years later and spending $400/mo less. On the example (64, $20,000 saved, $9,000/mo spending, SS $2,400 from 67, retire 65, plan to 90): retiring at 65 gives 0% at EVERY spending level tested down to $2,200/mo — because the two years before Social Security starts drain the whole pot — while retiring at 67 on $2,400/mo gives 100%, and the most they could spend from 67 is ~$2,450. The binding constraint was never 'spend less', it was the GAP before guaranteed income starts, which no lever tests. So the app already knew a specific true actionable sentence and was rendering an empty box. Nest egg needed for $9,000/mo from 65 = $1,810,000 with SS counted ($2,380,000 without). MOCK (mock-first, not built): low-odds-honest-sentence-v1-2026-08-13.html — Plan, Home and Net worth, with a sourcing table for every figure. FLOOR PROPOSED under 5% (1% and 3% are as useless as 0) — founder to confirm. NEW ENGINE WORK: the earliest retirement age that works, and the spending level that works from it. FLAGGED IN THE MOCK: this is the ONE place the app replaces a true number with prose, and it is a deliberate softening that should be chosen on purpose. ALSO OPEN: whether the free routes name actual organisations (safe for non-profits/government, unlike firms) — no commercial referrals, no named advice firms in v1.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-13, item 6 of the one-at-a-time audit walk. The 'who is that someone' question was answered as: name the KIND (fee-only, hourly) never a firm, because someone with $20,000 is below the minimum most percentage-of-assets advisers accept — 'a financial advisor' would send the person who needs help most to a door that will not open.

rows.means: Founder caught that the three 'things that cost nothing' rows in mock v1 had arrows and NO DESTINATIONS — the same mistake as the mortgage row, made twice in one session. Verified all three on the web today rather than from memory. (1) BENEFITSCHECKUP, benefitscheckup.org, run by the National Council on Aging: free, confidential, no registration, ZIP code + a few questions, nearly 2,000 programmes (food, medicine, utilities, heating) across all 50 states + DC; HELPLINE 1-800-794-6559 Mon-Fri 8am-7pm ET; Spanish at BuscaBeneficios.org. (2) SHIP, shiphelp.org, State Health Insurance Assistance Program: 'one-on-one counseling from a trusted, unbiased source', funded by the Administration for Community Living (US HHS), with a Find Your Local SHIP locator for all 50 states + Puerto Rico, Guam, USVI. (3) NFCC, nfcc.org, National Foundation for Credit Counseling: non-profit since 1951, 1,500+ certified counsellors, FREE financial action plan, phone 877-360-6322, 4-star Charity Navigator. TWO CHANGES THE VERIFICATION FORCED, neither of which I knew when drawing v1: (a) PHONE NUMBERS GO ON THE ROWS — two of the three run staffed helplines, and for someone in their late sixties who has just been told they cannot retire, a number to call likely beats a web form; the handoff sheet gains a 'Call instead' button beside 'Open'. (b) SHIP LINKS TO THE LOCATOR, not the homepage — help is state-by-state and a landing page would make them hunt. PATTERN: row -> one reusable handoff sheet (what the place is + 'we have no relationship with them and we get nothing if you use it' + Open / Call / Not now) -> browser. STILL OPEN: the fee-only row has NO destination on purpose — adviser directories are membership bodies with commercial interests of their own, unlike the three above, so picking one is a different kind of decision and needs research + a founder call. rows.his_words: yes to both
rows.plain: His answer: “yes to both”. The “Add a big cost” door comes back to the foot of the big one-time costs section, matching the row the design already drew — a screen that exists and cannot be reached is a screen nobody has.
rows.means: Founder: 'yes to both'. THE INSTANCE: '＋ Add a big cost ›' returns to the foot of the BIG ONE-TIME COSTS section on the Plan tab (PlanInputs -> /big-costs), matching the row Claude Design's v3 already draws so it converges with the redesign. Root cause, mine: on 2026-08-12 three things moved off the tab and the commit claimed all three landed in section 1 — two did, the big-costs door did not, leaving a fully built, registered, working screen reachable from NOWHERE in the app, while the section itself warned that leaving costs out distorts the odds. THE CLASS: new src/__tests__/orphan_route_guard.test.ts — every registered route must have an inbound link from somewhere a person can tap. The forward direction was already guarded (no button may point at a non-existent route); the reverse had nothing, which is why this sat invisible. Verified to bite: remove the door and it goes red naming /big-costs. IMPORTANT SELF-CORRECTION — my first version of the guard scanned only screens/ and components/ and reported SEVEN orphans, THREE of them false: /contribution-room, /worth-a-look and /idle-cash are reached from INSIGHT CARDS, which carry a `route` field and live in src/domain/insights, and /savings is reached from the onboarding summary. The guard now scans all of src. A guard that looks in too few places is worse than none — it cries wolf and gets muted. The three genuine orphans (/income, /invest, /income-detail) are listed BY NAME in the guard with the founder's 2026-08-02 'keep ALL orphans' ruling and its reason (future age groups), so deleting one remains a founder call rather than a tidy-up. Gates: 1623 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. OPEN: whether big costs also earns a ☰ menu entry as a permanent second way in.

rows.his_words: fix it now
rows.plain: His instruction: “fix it now”. The target rows and the target-reaching sentences stand down for someone already retired. A target is a “will I get there” question; once you are drawing down, the question is whether it lasts.
rows.means: Founder: 'fix it now'. The target rows and both target-reaching sentences now stand down for the retired lens. A target is a 'will I get there' framing; once you are drawing down the question is 'is this covering me', and the paycheck answers it. That was adopted when the Claude Design handoff arrived and reconfirmed 2026-08-13 when the founder chose the paycheck for June's second dial — it had simply never been built. BEFORE, measured on June's corrected numbers: 'On track for $985,000 · Target nest egg $400,000 · More than you need $585,000', then 'You've cleared the 80% mark — nothing more to put away to stay there', then four lines later '~$2,336,000 to spare'. TWO SPARE FIGURES on one screen measuring different things (today's money against a target pot; the median left at 94), neither labelled as which, and a woman who is not saving being told to put nothing more away. AFTER: the odds, then a single spare figure on the line that also carries her 1.9% withdrawal rate. The impossible-state levers block is deliberately KEPT for retirees — spending less and claiming later still move a retiree's odds, so that is not target framing. Pinned by 5 tests including one proving a working-lens person is unaffected. Converges with the redesign, whose June frames carry no target rows either. NOTED WHILE LOOKING, not part of D8: that same line still says 'within the safe range' — the banned-word sweep the founder approved (29 places, 14 files) is still pending. Gates: 1628 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: withdrawal should be next to amount you are withdrawing not amount you will spare.
rows.plain: His words: “withdrawal should be next to amount you are withdrawing not amount you will spare.” He is right, and the code confirmed it — the rate is worked out from what you draw, so it belongs beside that figure and not beside the leftover.
rows.means: Founder 2026-08-13: 'withdrawal should be next to amount you are withdrawing not amount you will spare.' He is right and the code confirms it: withdrawalPlan() computes (spending − guaranteed income) ÷ savings, so for June the 1.9% describes the $1,600 a month she draws — a figure that appeared NOWHERE in the sentence carrying the rate. It had been tacked on to the retired summary line beside '~$2,336,000 to spare': a rate measuring money going OUT, printed next to money staying IN. MOVED to the paycheck card, immediately after the draw it divides. The line now reads: '✓ covers your $5,600/mo spending. You're drawing $1,600 a month — 1.9% of your savings a year, within the ~4% guideline. You could draw up to $4,155.' Three clean clauses; an earlier draft read 'drawing $1,600 of the $4,155 you could, 1.9%…' which let a reader attach the rate to the wrong figure. The rate now also appears on the OVERSPENDING branch, where it matters more and was previously absent. NEW HELPER rateWords() replaces the inline band phrasing and drops the banned word — 'within the safe range' → 'within the ~4% guideline', 'watch it' → 'worth watching', 'high risk of running short' → 'a high chance of running short'. Applied HERE ONLY because the line was being rewritten anyway and re-typing a banned word into new code is not defensible; the full sweep the founder approved is still outstanding (27 occurrences remain, including 'Safe draw from savings' three lines above this very fix). Pinned: the rate must be adjacent to the draw and must NOT appear on the to-spare line. Gates: 1629 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. LESSON: a JSX comment cannot sit inside a ternary branch — it becomes a second expression and the file stops parsing.

rows.his_words: I am good with plan v3
rows.plain: The heading rule, approved: a FILLED dark-green band is reserved for a group that carries its own total on the right. A section without a total gets a quieter capitals label instead. So a filled band always means “there is a total here”.
rows.means: Founder: 'I am good with plan v3'. THE RULE, from Plan-v3-requirements.md: a FILLED deep-green band is reserved for a group carrying its own TOTAL on the right edge; a SECTION TITLE is a quiet caps label with no fill; everything else is a plain row. Root cause was never a Plan-tab bug — the app had exactly ONE heading style (the band adopted 2026-08-04, used across 35 files) and the Plan tab has seven things that need naming, so every one became a full-width green bar and nothing was emphasised because everything was. MEASURED: 7 filled bands -> 2, and the survivors are precisely the two with totals riding them. DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM THE v3 NOTE: it specifies the quiet label in mid brand green #178F6B, which measures 3.78:1 on the #F6F7F5 background and fails the 4.5:1 floor for small text — that was blocker B6 in my handoff review, and building it as specified would have shipped the defect I had just flagged. Built in #085041 (8.74:1), the same lesson the theme file already records for the band itself. SCOPE: Plan only. The prop is optional and defaults off, so the other 34 files are untouched BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by care. Net worth would not change regardless — its bands are genuine section headers with totals, which is exactly what the filled band is for under the new rule. A wider sweep of the remaining screens stays a deliberate founder call, not a side effect. PINNED in plan_appearance_audit: every filled band must carry a money figure, at most three may exist, and the quiet label must be the accessible green at 11px. Gates: 1631 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. NOTE FOR THE FILE RECORD: the v3 handoff lives in 'A-instructions for claude/design_handoff_net_worth 3/' — the older 'Plan screen/' folder still holds the SUPERSEDED v2 design and its requirements note (derived target, the deleted verdict words, the $1.9M bridge sentence), with nothing marking it stale. Retiring/renaming those folders is still an open founder call.

rows.his_words: We have built a lot of features but we are missing proper organization
rows.plain: His words: “We have built a lot of features but we are missing proper organization.” He asked for a map of every screen — where each one can be reached from today, and where it should live — so a screen that is built and reachable from nowhere cannot hide.
rows.means: Founder: 'We have built a lot of features but we are missing proper organization' → asked for a Figma-style architecture of where every screen is reachable from today and where it should live, to eliminate future rework, and chose the GENERATED option over a drawing. NEW scripts/screen-map.mjs reads the code (routes from the filesystem, every inbound link across all of src and app, the tab bar from constants/tabs.ts, each screen's own opening comment as its purpose) and renders docs/FCC-core-55-70/screen-architecture.html. THREE VIEWS: A = as it is today, MEASURED, every screen colour-coded well-connected / one door / only-if-an-insight-fires / no way in; B = what should move, AUTHORED and labelled as a recommendation; C = the decisions the founder still owes. The two halves are deliberately separated so opinion is never mistaken for a fact about the codebase. WHAT IT FOUND: 5 screens with NO WAY IN ((tabs)/tips, (tabs)/rewards, income, income-detail, invest — the last three are recorded founder keeps, the first two are debt); 4 reachable ONLY conditionally (contribution-room, idle-cash, worth-a-look via insights, and /savings which is linked only from the onboarding summary, so no existing user can open it); 8 hanging on a SINGLE door, which is exactly how /big-costs broke. PLAN SUB-TABS recorded in brief v3 §3.0: Retire (+ what-if moved in from Performance, + contribution-room given a permanent home), Goals (+ multi-goal promoted to its front door), Prepare (insurance, estate, tax organiser, credit, stress test, job safety). Prepare is largely a NAME for something that already exists — the Goals screen quietly links five of those today. DEFECTS FOUND IN MY OWN TOOLING WHILE BUILDING IT, all fixed: the route guard was too narrow for the THIRD time — it read _layout's <Stack.Screen> declarations, which cover only about half the live routes, so 23 routes were never checked at all (now reads the disk, since routing is file-based); door patterns conflated /invest with /(tabs)/invest, crediting a dead legacy screen with the live Performance tab's doors and hiding a real orphan; the route guard's own allowlist was being counted as a door; and domain-layer doors were labelled 'index' and 'hub', which tells a reader nothing. NEW CROSS-CHECK TEST: the generated map and the orphan guard must agree on what is unreachable — two independent readings forced to match, which also makes a stale committed map fail the suite. VERIFIED: output is byte-identical across runs; a planted door-less screen is caught and clears once given a door; three screens spot-checked by hand against the code. Registered in docs/README.md; regeneration added to the pre-build checklist in CLAUDE.md. Gates: 1633 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. NOTHING REORGANISED YET — the map is a decision aid; the moves await founder rulings.

rows.his_words: route key unchanged
rows.plain: He read the first screen map and caught three faults. The worst: it printed the internal route names, which had deliberately never been renamed when the tabs were — so the page looked as though the tab rename had been forgotten. The map now uses human names and plain-English purposes.
rows.means: Founder read the first version and caught three things. (1) THE PAGE LOOKED LIKE THE TAB RENAME HAD BEEN FORGOTTEN — it printed raw route keys, and those were deliberately never renamed when the tabs were (constants/tabs.ts: `invest` IS the Performance tab, `analytics` IS Net worth, 'route key unchanged'). Every box now leads with the name a person sees and keeps the route beneath it as the technical detail it is. CHECKED THE APP ITSELF while answering: there is NO stale 'Invest' copy anywhere in the user-visible strings — the 2026-08-04 rename was applied properly. Two harmless leftovers: a code comment in IdleCashScreen, and two lines in RetirementCockpit saying 'the Net Worth tab' where the bar says 'Net worth' (capitalisation, not a rename miss). (2) 'WHAT DOES EACH SCREEN DO?' — the page was showing each screen's opening code comment, which is engineer's notes ('Phase B', 'Mock C', 'GROUPED BY THEME') and often truncated mid-sentence. Added an AUTHORED one-line description for all 48, in plain English, with the code comment kept as a fallback and a warning printed for any screen missing one so the list cannot rot. (3) NEW SECTION D — every screen in one table: what it does, where it lives, and whether it moves. 33 of 48 stay exactly where they are, 9 move, 6 await a ruling. Section C decisions now also say what the screens involved actually do (Tips = short money tips, Rewards = points and streaks, both written for a younger audience; /savings = the onboarding savings engine; monthly income = where Social Security, pension and annuity get entered). Legacy screens no longer say 'stays' in the moving column — they say 'awaiting your ruling', which is the truth. Gates: 1633 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed; output verified byte-identical across runs.

rows.his_words: under cashflow I don
rows.plain: His words: “under cashflow I don’t see spending and debt tabs.” A REAL BLIND SPOT, not a missing screen: a sub-tab is a state inside a screen rather than a screen of its own, so a map built from screens could not see it. The map now shows sub-tabs.
rows.means: Founder: 'under cashflow I don't see spending and debt tabs.' A REAL BLIND SPOT, not a missing screen: sub-tabs are state INSIDE a screen, not routes, so a route-based map cannot see them. Cash flow has four (This month · Income · Spending · Debts), Net worth has two (By class · By institution), and the proposed Plan split has three — all invisible on the first version, which made the app look thinner than it is. FIX: the SCREENS that have sub-tabs are declared by hand (an array of labels cannot be told apart from an input control automatically — ['weekly','biweekly','monthly'] is a frequency picker, not navigation), and the LABELS are then read out of the code, so adding a tab updates the page on the next run. Net worth is the exception and its labels are written down: its array holds internal keys ['type','account'] with the labels computed in a ternary beside them, so reading the source would have shown a reader plumbing instead of what the tabs say. The proposed Retire · Goals · Prepare split renders on the Plan box in a distinct style, marked 'proposed', so what exists and what is suggested are never confused. Sub-tabs also appear in the every-screen table. NEW WARNING with a guard against its own noise: any tab-shaped array that is neither declared a sub-tab nor recorded as something else gets reported, and the seven existing non-navigation arrays are each recorded with a reason (filter chips, frequency pickers, the Simple/Advisor lens switch). A warning that fires on things already decided is noise, and noise gets muted — which is precisely how the orphan guard went unheeded three times. Gates: 1633 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed, output byte-identical across runs.
