rows.his_words: the latest home screen in last build does not link to insights or sharpen your plan.
rows.plain: “the latest home screen in last build does not link to insights or sharpen your plan.” Verified in the code — Home linked to NEITHER. The map was regrouped by where a screen can ACTUALLY be reached from, rather than by where it was supposed to sit.
rows.means: FOUNDER FOUND A REAL FLAW IN MY DOCUMENT: 'the latest home screen in last build does not link to insights or sharpen your plan.' Verified in code — HomeScreen links to NEITHER. Insights is reachable only from the ☰ menu; Sharpen only from the Plan tab, will-it-last and an insight card. The map was not wrong on the facts (the door line under each box said so) but its STRUCTURE lied: View A was labelled 'as it is today — measured' and yet grouped by each screen's PROPOSED home, so Insights and Sharpen sat inside a box headed 'Home'. Same defect I flagged in the design handoff's gauges — a shape saying one thing while the small print says another, and the eye believes the shape. FIXED: View A now groups by WHERE A PERSON ACTUALLY FINDS IT, measured — the tab bar itself (5) · from Home (3) · from Net worth (5) · from Performance (3) · from Cash flow (3) · from Plan (6) · from the ☰ menu (10) · deeper in, from another screen (4) · only when the data offers it (4) · nowhere (5) · second routes and redirects (3). Where View A and the proposal disagree, THAT GAP IS THE FINDING, and the caption now says so. NEW THING THE REGROUPING REVEALS: TEN screens hang off the ☰ menu alone — Goals, Retirement, Settings, Education, Estate, Insurance, Tax organiser, Stress test, Expense, Insights. FOUNDER DECISION SAME MESSAGE: 'I do agree insights, and sharpen both belong on the home screen' — both recorded as agreed moves in the map (Insights: menu → Home; Sharpen: Plan → Home). NOT BUILT: adding links to Home is a screen change and the mock-first standing order applies. Count now reads 31 of 48 stay, 11 move, 6 await a ruling. Gates: 1633 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed, output stable across runs.

rows.his_words: For home screen - let
rows.plain: Four rulings about where screens live, all four recorded in the screen map and held by a test. The first: TIPS AND REWARDS are saved for future use, so they move from the list of screens nobody can reach into the list of deliberate keeps. THE STRANDED LIST IS NOW EMPTY — which is the point of it: an entry there means nobody can reach this screen and nobody decided that.
rows.means: FOUNDER RULINGS, all four recorded in the screen map and the guard: (1) TIPS AND REWARDS — saved for future use, so they move from the stranded register to the deliberate keeps beside /income, /invest and /income-detail. THE STRANDED REGISTER IS NOW EMPTY, which is the point of it: an entry there means 'nobody can reach this and nobody has decided whether that is on purpose' — a question, not a resting place. (2) MONTHLY INCOME — lens-dependent, and a genuinely sharp distinction: for someone RETIRED this is their actual income so it belongs in Cash flow › Income; for someone still WORKING it is a future number they are planning around so it belongs in Plan › Retire. Same screen, two homes, decided by the lens the app already switches on. (3) PLAN KEEPS THREE SUB-TABS — founder's reason recorded: easy access to features without overcrowding one screen or burying them in the menu. (4) EIGHT SINGLE-DOOR SCREENS — accepted, now that the guard catches the moment one loses its last door. ALSO: View A of the map was regrouped by where screens are ACTUALLY reached from (see previous row), which revealed that ten screens hang off the ☰ menu alone. HOME BRIEF WRITTEN: mockups/Home-redesign-Aug-13/HOME-REDESIGN-BRIEF-v1-2026-08-13.md, built on a fresh DUMP of the shipping screen (new src/__tests__/home_dump.test.tsx — never write a brief from memory). What the dump found and the brief now carries: (a) Home already shows 'CHIEF OF STAFF — WHAT NEEDS YOU (3)', three ranked insight cards, and June's third card literally reads 'One thing would sharpen every number' — so the founder's Insights and Sharpen links are NOT a blank space to fill; the real question is how that block relates to the fuller Insights screen without becoming a duplicate list, and the brief poses it that way. (b) THE BANNED WORD IS JUNE'S HERO — 'SAFE TO SPEND — AUG' and 'Safe draw from savings'. (c) TWO NUMBERS ARGUE: her hero says $8,155 spendable and four lines later warns 'this draw is above what your own numbers support long-term' — both true, measured against different standards (80% odds vs the 4% guideline; hers is 5.1%), and a person cannot tell which to believe. (d) the page-level disclaimer claims her own reported Social Security is an estimate. (e) Home runs to 49 lines for Pat and 65 for June, so the brief demands the designer say what they REMOVED. Four states requested including the part-way state nobody has ever drawn. Gates: 1636 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: Since we are going to label this tab Retire under Plan (parent tab). We can drop your retirement plan heading.
rows.plain: “Since we are going to label this tab Retire under Plan (parent tab). We can drop your retirement plan heading.” The heading is gone — it sat directly above “WILL MY MONEY LAST?” saying nearly the same thing twice.
rows.means: Founder: 'Since we are going to label this tab Retire under Plan (parent tab). We can drop your retirement plan heading.' The heading is gone — it sat directly above 'WILL MY MONEY LAST?' saying nearly the same thing, and the heavy green bars had disguised that until the D9 hierarchy change turned both into quiet labels. With the tab itself named Retire under Plan, the card need not announce which tab it is on; the question is the heading. THE ALIGNMENT HALF WENT DEEPER THAN THE FINDING: my first fix made the quiet label IGNORE `inCard`, and measuring proved that only moved the problem — headings outside a card then sat 12pt left of those inside, with 'DECISIONS YOU CAN MAKE TODAY' the odd one out. The flag does carry the fact that matters (whether a card's padding already sits to the left), so a quiet label now adds ONE inset inside a card and TWO outside, putting every heading on the same line as every row. Every quiet band in the Plan surface was audited for which side of that it falls on. Measured: six headings at [24, 12] → all six at 24. PINNED so it cannot drift: the set of heading left-edges must have exactly one member, and the dropped heading is pinned absent. rows.his_words: . FACT moves off the light green band tint onto the neutral tint. Why it matters more than a badge normally would: FACT means
rows.plain: “do it”. The FACT badge moves off the green tint onto a neutral one. It matters more than a badge usually would, because FACT means “this is saved” and DRAFT means “you are only trying this” — and two badges that look alike make a person think a change is saved when it is not.
rows.means: Founder: 'do it'. FACT moves off the light green band tint onto the neutral tint. Why it matters more than a badge normally would: FACT means 'this is saved' and DRAFT means 'you are only trying this, nothing has changed' — that pair IS the facts-save / choices-commit model the Plan tab is built on. Both were two shades of the same light green, so the badge carried no information and a person had to stop and READ the word to learn whether their answer had been committed, which is the one job a badge exists to spare them. Claude Design had specified it correctly and we built it wrong; their note reads 'FACT tag: neutral chip… this colour distinction is the primary way a person tells facts from choices at a glance.' PINNED: the three chips (FACT / DRAFT / MISSING) must sit on different colour families, with FACT explicitly on the neutral tint and explicitly NOT on the green band tint it used to wear; and the quiet chip's contrast is RECOMPUTED from the live tokens inside the test, so a future palette change that drops it below the 4.5:1 small-text floor fails rather than ships (4.60:1 today). DEFERRED BY AGREEMENT to Claude Design's redraw: the badges are not real pills — they are words with a background whose inset is faked with blank spaces, because a nested Text cannot take padding reliably in React Native. Fine at default type, drifts apart when a reader turns their text size up, which this audience does. NOTE: the colour-token guard failed the first attempt because I had written raw hex codes into a code comment explaining the contrast — it cannot tell a comment from a style and was right to fail; the number lives in the test now. Gates: 1640 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: s 401(k) insight and the contribution-room screen. THE FOUNDER
rows.plain: The sentence telling you how much of the saving you need fits somewhere tax-advantaged had been written and then fed an empty value, so it could never appear at all. It is connected up and now uses a real figure.
rows.means: The sentence that tells someone how much of the required saving fits somewhere tax-advantaged had been written and then fed a hard-coded undefined, so it could never render. Wired now, using a figure the app already computes for Home's 401(k) insight and the contribution-room screen. THE FOUNDER'S QUESTION IS WHAT MADE THIS MORE THAN A WIRE-UP: 'How do we know person has not already taken advantage of 401K contributions?' Checked the engine — the headroom is the IRS limit minus what the person TOLD US they contribute monthly, times twelve. It does subtract contributions, but it assumes that figure held evenly across the whole year, which is wrong for anyone who front-loaded, started or stopped mid-year, changed job, or defers a bonus, and it never sees an employer match. We read no payroll or plan statement; there is no source of truth for what has actually gone in. Over-contributing to a 401(k) carries a real tax penalty, so stating an estimate as a fact about someone's allowance is not acceptable. FOUNDER RULED the hedged wording: 'About $32,500 of that should fit in tax-advantaged room, going by the $800 a month you told us you already put in.' THE CLASS WAS FIXED, NOT THE INSTANCE: the same unhedged claim was already live in two other places and both are corrected — Home's insight and the contribution-room screen now name the source and, on the screen, tell the person to check it against their latest statement. The sentence stays silent when no contribution figure was ever given, rather than guessing, and retirees never see it. Pinned three ways including the silent case; a stale pin asserting the old unhedged wording was updated with the reason beside it. Gates: 1641 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: What drives this? ›
rows.plain: “What drives this?” was a tap target about 19 points tall against the 44-point minimum that exists for exactly this audience. Raised to 44. A link too small to hit reliably is a link that is not there.
rows.means: 'What drives this? ›' was a single 15pt line in a touchable with no height and no padding — about 19pt of target against the 44pt rule that exists for exactly this audience. Raised to 44 with the text centred. The other five things the measurement flagged were checked and are fine: the decision rows, the next-decision card and the Sharpen card all clear 44 once their own content is counted (58-62pt). THE CHECK ITSELF HAD THREE DEFECTS, all found by trying to make it fail instead of trusting a green tick: it read only minHeight and padding, so the stepper buttons — declared a flat 44x44 via `height` — were reported as 19pt targets that do not exist; it required a style prop, so a touchable with NO style was skipped entirely, which is precisely how a 19pt target arises, meaning the check walked straight past its own subject; and it sat outside the describe that seeds the persona, so it rendered the FIRST-DAY screen where the link is absent and passed without looking at anything. Fixed, then verified by reverting the code fix — the pin goes red naming 'What drives this? › ≈ 19pt'. THIS CLOSES ALL 15 AUDIT FINDINGS from the 2026-08-12 mock-match audit. STILL OPEN AND APP-WIDE, deliberately not folded in: the ⓘ info dot is a 13pt glyph with 6/4 padding, roughly 21pt, with no hitSlop. It sits on most screens, so raising it is one change in one component — but padding would shift layout and hitSlop on a React Native Text is not reliably supported, so it needs a decision and a device check rather than a quiet edit. Gates: 1642 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: info dot should be the same size as text. Can we do that?
rows.plain: “info dot should be the same size as text. Can we do that?” Yes — and it is a better answer than making it bigger. The dot was a flat 13 points everywhere regardless of the text beside it, so next to a heading it looked lost and next to small print it looked oversized. It now matches its neighbour.
rows.means: Founder: 'info dot should be the same size as text. Can we do that?' Yes, and it is a better answer than making it bigger. The dot was a FLAT 13pt at all 30 call sites regardless of its neighbour — so it loomed over an 11pt band title and shrank beside a 30pt hero. It now takes a `size` prop; SectionBand passes its own title size (11), which covers the most visible mismatch across many screens since band titles are the smallest text in the app. Remaining call sites default to 13, which is the common row size. Pinned two ways: the dot takes the size it is given, and a band's dot equals that band's title size — read from the rendered styles, so the two cannot drift. THE TAP AREA IS A SEPARATE PROBLEM AND IS DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. At 11pt the touchable is roughly 19pt against the 44pt rule. I tried hitSlop — it grows a touch region without moving a pixel of layout — and THE TYPECHECK REFUSED IT: hitSlop does not exist on Text in React Native 0.85. That is how we know rather than guess, and the attempt was removed rather than shipped unverifiable. The remaining options each cost something and need a founder call plus a device check: a wrapping Pressable renders a button, and these dots frequently sit inside tappable cards where a button nested in a button is invalid on web (the reason the component is a pressable Text in the first place); more padding grows every row that carries a dot. Recorded in the component so the next person meets the reasoning, not the symptom. Gates: 1644 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.his_words: s constraint, stated plainly:
rows.plain: “the height of the info dot circle should match the height of the text size. that way we are not stretching height of the row for info dot as that would look unprofessional.” So the dot stays the size of its text, and the 44-point tap area is achieved by extending the INVISIBLE touch area around it — the row height never changes.
rows.means: Founder's constraint, stated plainly: 'the height of the info dot circle should match the height of the text size. that way we are not stretching height of the row for info dot as that would look unprofessional.' Built exactly that. The GLYPH is drawn at the size of the text beside it (11pt on a band title, 13 on a row). The TOUCH box is carried to 44pt by padding, and an equal NEGATIVE MARGIN hands that space straight back to the layout — so the net footprint is exactly the glyph and a row carrying a dot is the same height as one without. The padding is computed from the size, so the box reaches 44 whatever the dot is drawn at. WHY NOT THE OBVIOUS TOOLS: hitSlop does not exist on Text in React Native 0.85 and the typecheck rejects it — that is how we know rather than guess; a wrapping Pressable renders a button, and these dots frequently sit inside tappable cards where a button nested in a button is invalid on web, which is the original reason this component is a pressable Text. PINNED three ways: the glyph takes the size it is given; the touch box computes to at least 44 at 11, 13 and 15pt; and the net footprint is ZERO vertically and exactly the 6pt visible gap horizontally — so a future edit that grows the row fails rather than ships. DEVICE CHECK STILL OWED and recorded in the component: a negative margin can be clipped by a parent that hides overflow, and Android does not always deliver touches past a parent's bounds. On the next build, tap one dot on a green band, one beside a hero number, and one inside a card that is itself tappable — that last is where clipping would show. Gates: 1646 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed.

rows.plain: “agree — keep the dials and shrink them.” This settles a contradiction inside the design handoff itself, which removed BOTH dials from the expanded view. They stay, smaller.
rows.means: Founder: 'agree - keep the dials and shrink them.' Settles a contradiction inside the Claude Design v3 handoff itself: the drawing removed BOTH dials from Pat's expanded frame, replacing them with a single line of text, while the accompanying requirements note stated the dials 'never move'. Verified against the file on disk — the collapsed frame carries 2 dials, the expanded frame carries 0. The founder ruled for the note. THE REASON MATTERS MORE THAN THE PIXELS: watching the odds respond is the entire point of putting the inputs on the tab instead of behind a link. A person nudges the retirement age in order to see what it does; with the dials gone they are adjusting numbers blind and then scrolling back up to find out what happened — a taller screen AND a worse one. So the dials shrink and stay, with the number being changed and the number it is being changed for on screen together. How small, and whether they pin or compress in place, left to the designer. Recorded in brief v3 §3.2 and struck off the handoff review's open list — four of its five rulings remain.

rows.his_words: Try all three together — one sandbox ›
rows.plain: The design ended its bad-odds screen with “Try all three together — one sandbox”, pointing at a sandbox he had already folded into this tab. The link is dropped — it pointed at a screen that no longer exists separately.
rows.means: Founder agreed the recommendation. The v3 handoff ends its bad-odds frame with 'Try all three together — one sandbox ›', pointing at the what-if sandbox the founder folded into this tab on 2026-08-12 — the steppers ARE the sandbox now, so the link has no destination. VERIFIED IT WAS NEVER BUILT: the phrase appears nowhere in src/, only in the drawing, so nothing ships broken today and no code changes. Same defect class as the mortgage row and the three free-route rows — an arrow with nothing behind it — except this one sits on the screen where the person is already in the most trouble. THE IDEA IS KEPT, THE LINK IS NOT: 'what if I did two or three of these at once' is a real question, but today the screen could only honour two of the three, since retiring later and spending less are steppers while claiming Social Security at 70 is not. A link that half-delivers on the worst screen in the app is worse than one fewer option. Recorded in brief v3 §5 as something the redesign may offer properly, with the condition that it must honour all three and say what it needs. Struck off the handoff review — three of its five rulings remain.

rows.his_words: IT should show for people between age group 60 and 67
rows.plain: “IT should show for people between age group 60 and 67” — then, once I flagged what stopping at 67 costs, “60 to 70 it is”. THE FLAG THAT CHANGED IT: between 67 and 70 the credit for delaying keeps building, so ending the decision at 67 hides the years where waiting pays most.
rows.means: Founder: 'IT should show for people between age group 60 and 67' → then, after I flagged what 67 costs, '60 to 70 it is'. THE FLAG THAT CHANGED IT: between 67 and 70 the delayed credit keeps accruing at 8% a year, so on a $2,600 statement the choice is worth $624 a month for life — and the row only ever shows to someone who has NOT claimed, so a 68-year-old seeing it genuinely still has it open. Stopping at 67 would have removed the decision at the moment it is worth most. THIS WAS A LIVE DEFECT, not just a brief note: nextDecision's only bound was age < 71 and the decision ROWS had no age gate at all, so Pat at 58 was being told the next decision in front of him was a claim window opening in 2030 — precisely what the founder ruled out on 2026-08-12. Now gated 60-70 in one place (SS_DECISION_FROM / SS_DECISION_TO in domain/planning/hub) and read by both the card and every row. PINNED in a new suite: not in your fifties, live 60 through 70, gone after 70, 68 explicitly included, and never shown to someone already drawing. A stale pin asserting the OLD behaviour — that a woman born in 1991 should see 'your claim window opens Aug 2053' — was updated to assert absence, with the ruling recorded beside it. BRIEF GAINS A THIRD PERSON: the row was drawn nowhere in the v3 handoff because Pat is 58 and June is 72 and already claiming, so neither could trigger it — MY gap, not the designer's. Ray, 64, still working part-time, not yet claimed, $2,600 statement. He is worth having beyond this row: the brief had a 58-year-old and a 72-year-old for an audience of 55 to 70, and the middle — where the biggest decisions get made — was missing entirely. Gates: 1652 green, tsc clean, UI gate passed. Two handoff rulings remain.

rows.his_words: i like your recommendation.
rows.plain: “i like your recommendation.” The design ended its age-missing screen with “Decisions are hidden until your odds can be computed.” REJECTED — the decisions list stays visible, because hiding it is hiding the very thing a person came to see.
rows.means: Founder: 'i like your recommendation.' The v3 handoff ends its age-missing frame with 'Decisions are hidden until your odds can be computed.' Rejected, and the founder's own decision list is the proof: PAYING OFF THE MORTGAGE EARLY NEEDS A MORTGAGE, NOT AN AGE; CONVERTING TO A ROTH NEEDS PRE-TAX MONEY, NOT AN AGE. Both work for someone who has linked accounts and skipped one question, and hiding them leaves an empty section where two actionable things belong — against this app's own rule that an empty state is an on-ramp, never a dead end. The rows that genuinely need an age already remove themselves after today's other rulings: Social Security is gated 60-70, the required withdrawal 73+. VERIFIED THE BUILT APP ALREADY DOES THIS — the missing-age render shows a locked 'When can I retire? 🔒' plus the decisions that apply — so this is a brief instruction to the designer, not a code change. KEPT FROM THE HANDOFF'S INSTINCT: the locked row is right, because that question truly cannot be answered without an age. A lock explains itself; an empty section does not. The designer's counter-argument is recorded rather than dismissed: without odds a decision can only say what it is worth in dollars and years, not points — but the points figure is not wired for either row yet, so nothing is lost today, and dollars and years are the honest half. Four of the five handoff rulings are now closed.

rows.his_words: hide the number, keep the shape.
rows.plain: Under hide-balances the odds dial stays fully visible — the percentage and the arc both. Only the target amount in dollars is dotted out. Hiding your balances is about money figures, not about whether your plan is working.
rows.means: Founder: 'hide the number, keep the shape.' Under hide-balances the ODDS dial stays fully visible — '48% odds of lasting to age 90' is not money and gives nothing away. On the TARGET dial the numeral is replaced by dots while the arc still fills to where it would. MY RECOMMENDATION WAS DIFFERENT AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY DROPPED: I argued for hiding that dial outright, because its percentage is built entirely from two dollar figures ($909,152 ÷ $2,000,000) and the arc conveys the same ratio the numeral does — so the shape leaks what the dots conceal, and a privacy switch that half works is worse than one that is predictable. The founder made an informed choice; the brief now carries both the ruling and the reservation, so the next person reading it can see the trade rather than rediscover it. A REFINEMENT OFFERED, NOT ASSUMED: if the arc is the only thing left, it need not be precise — filling to a coarse band reads 'about this far along' while giving a shoulder-surfer much less than a needle at exactly 45%. Left to the designer to accept or reject with a stated reason. Nothing to build today: the two-dial hero is the redesign, and the built screen's money already masks. THIS CLOSES ALL FIVE HANDOFF-REVIEW RULINGS.

rows.means: Four sub-folders of Claude Design deliveries had accumulated outside the app, all named after net worth because that was the first screen drawn, though they now also hold the Performance and Plan handoffs. A byte-for-byte comparison showed three of the four contain nothing unique except a single file — the superseded v2 Plan drawing. Founder: rename the latest so the single source of truth is obvious. Now '00-CURRENT-handoff-Net-worth-Performance-Plan-2026-08-14' — it names all three screens it holds, carries its delivery date, and sorts to the top of the folder. Nothing was deleted: the older copies stay where they are, and the v2 Plan drawing is a genuine superseded version that the mock-first rule says must be kept. The v3 originals are now ON DISK and the handoff review was re-checked against them rather than the chat copies it was first written from: the files are clean (no character corruption) and finding B1 is confirmed to the decimal — the six gauge needles point at 56.3%, 97.4%, 64.5% and 4.6% beneath printed values of 48%, 100%, 84% and 12%, while the arcs behind them are correct at 45.2% and 13.3%. The review's warning that it might be reporting on corrupted copies is lifted.

rows.his_words: fixed it in one of six places
rows.plain: He ruled the Social Security claim decision belongs to ages 60 to 70. That had been applied on the Plan tab and NOT in Insights, which still used 62 to under-70 — the same decision behind two different gates, which is the exact fault the whole one-decision-one-place rule exists to stop. Now one gate, read from one place.
rows.means: The founder ruled the claim decision belongs to ages 60 to 70. That was applied on the Plan tab and NOT in Insights, which still used 62 to under-70 — the same decision, two different gates, the exact 'fixed it in one of six places' failure the full-surface rule exists to stop. BOTH ENDS WERE WRONG. At the young end, 60- and 61-year-olds got nothing, though that is the last stretch where the answer can still be planned around. At the old end the card vanished at exactly 70, which is the most urgent month of all: the delayed credit stops there, so from then on waiting costs money and buys nothing. Insights now reads the same two constants the Plan tab reads, so the two surfaces cannot drift apart again. ONE WORDING DECISION CAME WITH IT, AND IT IS FLAGGED FOR THE FOUNDER RATHER THAN ASSUMED: simply widening the gate to 60 would have shown a 60-year-old a card headed 'Your Social Security window is open' when it is not — it opens at 62. So the card now has two versions. At 60 and 61: 'Your Social Security decision is coming up — you can first claim at 62, and every year you wait after that raises the check, up to 70.' From 62: the existing 'window is open' wording, unchanged. Both lead to the same screen.
rows.why: Completes a ruling already given rather than new scope; the two new sentences need the founder to confirm the words.

rows.his_words: yes, I like the text.
rows.plain: “yes, I like the text.” The Social Security card is approved in two versions: at 60 and 61 it says the decision is coming up, that you can first claim at 62, and that every year you wait after that raises the amount — so the card is honest about what you cannot do yet.
rows.means: Founder: 'yes, I like the text.' The two-version card is approved and live. At 60 and 61: 'Your Social Security decision is coming up — you can first claim at 62, and every year you wait after that raises the check, up to 70. Worth deciding before it arrives.' From 62 onward the existing 'window is open' wording is unchanged. Both open the same screen. The changelog row logged earlier today as AWAITING founder confirmation is now settled. BRIEFS PREPARED TO SEND: the Plan brief now opens its 'what went wrong' section with a pointer to the handoff review and leads on the defect to fix first — all six gauge needles point at the wrong number (56/97/65/5 percent beneath printed 48/100/84/12) while the arcs behind them are correct, so we are asking for the angle formula rather than placed coordinates; it also marks the two review items that are ours rather than the designer's, and its deliverables now call for all three people. The Home brief is welded to the Plan brief so the same person cannot carry different figures on two screens: it takes every dollar from the Plan brief's persona section rather than re-deriving, asks for a Ray frame because his 'what needs you' block carries a card Pat's never shows, quotes the approved Social Security wording by age band, and now carries the hide-balances ruling across from the Plan surface with the reservation and the coarse-fill refinement stated.
rows.why: Closes the last wording gate; both briefs are now complete and internally consistent with each other.

rows.plain: “create a folder called August 14th Design, move the latest files there so there is no confusion, and re-check every file carries the decisions we made.” One named home for the live set, and every file in it re-checked against the decisions rather than assumed to carry them.
rows.means: Founder: create a folder called August 14th Design, move the latest files there so there is no confusion, and re-check every file carries the decisions we made. DONE, BOTH HALVES. The folder now holds the Plan brief (renamed to 2026-08-14 because its old name said the 12th while it had been revised materially today), the Home brief, the handoff review, Claude Design's own delivered files, and a README stating which file is live and what is deliberately absent. Superseded work stays where it is — brief v1 and v2 and the 08-12 review in mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/, three older Claude Design copies in A-instructions for claude/ — because the mock-first rule keeps old versions but does not keep them where they can be mistaken for current. Every reference to a moved file was repointed and checked. THE RE-CHECK WAS RUN AGAINST THE FILES, NOT FROM MEMORY: 32 decisions from this engagement were each tested for by searching the document or the source that should carry them. 31 passed on the first pass. ONE FAILED — the hide-balances ruling was described accurately in the Plan brief but did not quote the founder's own five words, 'hide the number, keep the shape', so a reader could not tell a ruling from my paraphrase of one. Now quoted identically in both briefs. Coverage: 32 of 32.
rows.why: The founder asked for confusion removed and the decisions verified; a check run from memory would have proved nothing.

rows.his_words: the safer basis
rows.plain: “do it as one sweep.” The word “safe” is removed from everything a person can read — 34 replacements across 16 files. “Safe to spend” becomes “LEFT TO SPEND”. Nothing in a plan is safe, and a word that promises safety is a promise the app cannot keep.
rows.means: Founder: do it as one sweep. DONE — 34 user-visible replacements across 16 files, using the wording already approved in brief v3 §7.1: Safe to spend → LEFT TO SPEND (the retiree hero on Home, the Cash flow heading, the month-detail heading and total, the 12 paycheck months and every spoken label behind them); Safe draw from savings → Draw from savings (the paycheck card, Plan hub, Cash flow, month detail, paycheck months, and the glossary entry every information dot on that line reads from); a safe pace → within the ~4% guideline; Your safety net → Your cushion (the job-safety screen heading and the reward badge); 'the safer basis' → 'the steadier basis' on the returns warning; and the first-run promise now says what's left to spend. OUT OF SCOPE ON PURPOSE, as the brief states: uses with nothing to do with money — 'your data is safe' after a failed import, 'I've saved my recovery code somewhere safe', the job-safety feature name, and internal code identifiers nobody reads. THE GUARD IS THE POINT, NOT THE SWEEP. A sweep only fixes today; src/__tests__/banned_word_guard.test.ts fails the build if the word reappears in any rendered string, label, title or spoken label in screens, components or domain. IT EARNED ITSELF IMMEDIATELY: it caught a visible section heading in month detail that still read SAFE TO SPEND, which my hand-sweep had walked straight past — a live demonstration that reading carefully is not a substitute for a gate. Suite 1665 green, typecheck clean, quality gate passing.
rows.why: Standing rule since 2026-08-12: we never call money safe, because we do not know and will not say anything binding.

rows.raw:
Founder: do it as one sweep. DONE — 34 user-visible replacements across 16 files, using the wording already approved in brief v3 §7.1: Safe to spend → LEFT TO SPEND (the retiree hero on Home, the Cash flow heading, the month-detail heading and total, the 12 paycheck months and every spoken label behind them); Safe draw from savings → Draw from savings (the paycheck card, Plan hub, Cash flow, month detail, paycheck months, and the glossary entry every information dot on that line reads from); a safe pace → within the ~4% guideline; Your safety net → Your cushion (the job-safety screen heading and the reward badge); 'the safer basis' → 'the steadier basis' on the returns warning; and the first-run promise now says what's left to spend. OUT OF SCOPE ON PURPOSE, as the brief states: uses with nothing to do with money — 'your data is safe' after a failed import, 'I've saved my recovery code somewhere safe', the job-safety feature name, and internal code identifiers nobody reads. THE GUARD IS THE POINT, NOT THE SWEEP. A sweep only fixes today; src/__tests__/banned_word_guard.test.ts fails the build if the word reappears in any rendered string, label, title or spoken label in screens, components or domain. IT EARNED ITSELF IMMEDIATELY: it caught a visible section heading in month detail that still read SAFE TO SPEND, which my hand-sweep had walked straight past — a live demonstration that reading carefully is not a substitute for a gate. Suite 1665 green, typecheck clean, quality gate passing.

WHY (from the source): Standing rule since 2026-08-12: we never call money safe, because we do not know and will not say anything binding.

rows.plain: He read the spend-more row and asked what the $5,600 meant — which found two defects in one line: the odds shown beside the control were not the odds for the amount the control was set to, and the figure itself was not labelled. A number on a screen that nobody can name is a defect even when it is right.
rows.means: Founder read June's spend-more row and asked what the $5,600 meant. Two defects in one line, both now written into brief §3.5 and logged as blocker B7 in the handoff review. FIRST, THE ODDS ARE WRONG AT THE DEFAULT AND CONTRADICT THE SAME SCREEN. The phrase 'held at odds of 80%' explains how the $2,555 was CALCULATED — the largest extra draw that still holds an 80% floor — and the brief attaches it to that figure. The handoff moved it onto the running total, where it is false everywhere except the far end. Measured on the engine: at $0 extra June is at 100%, still 100% at $500 and $1,000 extra, then 97% at $1,500, 90% at $2,000, and 80% only at the $2,555 maximum. As drawn, the screen would print 80% directly beneath a dial reading 100% for the identical plan — that reads as a broken app, not a nuance. The odds beside a live control must themselves be live, which is brief §6.1 (odds are only ever an output) applied to a stepper. The real curve is also a better answer than the static one: her first $1,000 a month costs her nothing, which is exactly what she came to that row to find out. SECOND, $5,600 IS UNLABELLED. At zero extra it is simply what she spends today, but an arrow pointing at it reads as the result of a decision she has not made; it needs naming at rest and becomes a '→ … in total' only once the control moves. The brief also now requires one sentence linking draw and spend — her guaranteed $4,000 does not change, so every extra dollar spent is an extra dollar drawn. Whole curve pinned in src/__tests__/june_numbers_probe.test.ts so the build cannot reintroduce a static odds figure. Nothing to build today: this control is the redesign, not shipped code.

rows.his_words: It is too complex for user to understand particularly someone with no finance background.
rows.plain: “too complex for someone with no finance background; put it in simple terms.” The spend-more row was rewritten in plain English and MOCKED rather than built, per the mock-first rule.
rows.means: Founder: too complex for someone with no finance background; put it in simple terms. MOCKED, NOT BUILT, per the mock-first rule — mockups/Plan-redesign-Aug-12/spend-more-plain-english-v1-2026-08-14.html, three full phone frames (as-drawn, plain at rest, plain pushed to the maximum) with every number taken from the engine and pinned by june_numbers_probe. THE DIAGNOSIS: the row made her work out four things unaided — what 'draw' means and how it differs from spend, why $2,555 is offered while $0 shows, what $5,600 is (it is what she already spends, and nothing said so), and what 'odds of 80%' refers to when the dial above reads 100%. THE REWRITE: the answer comes first and it is the free money — 'Yes, about $1,000 a month more, and nothing changes', because the engine's own curve holds 100% all the way to $1,000 extra. That was the single most useful fact on the row and the static 80% label was hiding it. Consequence is then stated as counts rather than percentages — 'your money lasts in about 4 futures out of 5, in the other 1 it runs out before 94' — because counts land with people who bounce off percentages, and the sentence names what happens in the losing case instead of leaving her to imagine it. One line closes the draw-versus-spend gap: 'Your Social Security and pension don't change, so anything extra comes out of savings.' WORDS REMOVED FROM THE ROW: draw, odds, held at, floor. WORDS KEPT: spend, month, lasts, runs out. NEEDS A FOUNDER CALL BEFORE IT GOES IN THE BRIEF: 'estimated amount you can draw more every month' is the founder's own wording and brief v3 §3.5 currently says it must not be softened or shortened. The mock removes it. That instruction is his to withdraw, not mine — the brief is unchanged until he says so.

rows.plain: “like B and C.” The plain-English version is approved. The row LEADS with the answer — “Yes, about $1,000 a month more, and nothing changes” — rather than making you read the working first.
rows.means: Founder: 'like B and C.' The plain-English frames are approved and are now brief §3.5 verbatim. The row leads with the answer — 'Yes, about $1,000 a month more, and nothing changes' — because the engine holds 100% all the way to $1,000 extra and that free headroom was the most useful fact on the row, buried under a static 80% label. Consequence is stated as a count with the losing case named: 'lasts in about 4 futures out of 5, in the other 1 it runs out before 94.' One sentence closes the draw-versus-spend gap. Words removed: draw, odds, held at, floor. THE FOUNDER'S OWN LINE IS WITHDRAWN BY THIS APPROVAL: 'estimated amount you can draw more every month' was his wording and the brief previously forbade softening it; frames B and C do not contain it, so approving them withdraws that instruction. Recorded explicitly rather than assumed, and reversible on a word from him. THE RULE GENERALISED RATHER THAN STOPPING AT ONE ROW (§3.5.1): wherever a decision row says what a choice does to the chance a plan works, it says it as a count out of a round number, never a percentage, and names what happens in the losing case. Applied on the spot to the MORTGAGE row, which ended 'your odds go from 48% to 43%' and now reads 'your money lasts in about 5 futures out of 10 today, and about 4 out of 10 if you do this' — same facts, and it finally says which way is worse. The Social Security row already passes and is named as the benchmark. One word left for the designer: 'pre-tax' on the Roth row, flagged with a suggested replacement rather than left alone.

rows.his_words: s move Pay off the mortgage early to Cash flow · Debt. It does not belong under Retire.
rows.plain: “let’s move Pay off the mortgage early to Cash flow · Debt. It does not belong under Retire.” Same control, drawn in a different place — it only ever sat under Retire because that is where it was first built.
rows.means: Founder: 'let's move Pay off the mortgage early to Cash flow · Debt. It does not belong under Retire.' Done in brief §3.3.1 — same control, drawn in a different place. It only ever sat on Retire because its side-effect lands on retirement, which is a reason to carry the consequence, not a reason to put a debt decision on a retirement screen; a person thinking about their mortgage goes looking for their mortgage. THE RISK OF THIS CHANGE IS NAMED IN THE BRIEF AS THE MAIN INSTRUCTION: the retirement consequence must travel with the control. Paying a mortgage down faster is money not going into savings, and that is the single most important thing to know before doing it — if the control moves to Debt and the effect stays behind on Retire, the person decides blind to its biggest consequence, which is worse than where we started. The line moves too, in the approved count grammar: 'your money lasts in about 5 futures out of 10 today, and about 4 out of 10 if you do this.' KNOCK-ON FLAGGED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: this leaves Pat with ONE decision row, since at 58 the Social Security row does not reach him for two years. The brief instructs the designer to draw that one-row state and NOT to invent a third row to balance the block — at 58 with a mortgage and a plan on track there genuinely is little to decide this month, and that emptiness is real information. Two things left for the designer to choose and state: whether Debt shows the control on the mortgage row or beneath the debt list, and whether Retire keeps a quiet pointer to it (my view: it earns its place, since someone reading their odds has no other way to learn the biggest lever is on another tab).

rows.his_words: It is too harsh.
rows.plain: “It is too harsh.” He was reading a line saying a 64-year-old will likely never close a $250,000 gap by saving $500 a month. He was right twice — it was harsh, and it was also wrong in the reassuring direction about his odds.
rows.means: Founder: 'It is too harsh.' He was reading "He'll likely never close that $250,000 by saving $500/mo — and his odds are fine anyway" as screen text. He was right twice. FIRST, HARSH: telling a 64-year-old he will never reach his retirement target is a projection dressed as a prophecy, and nobody should read that sentence about their own money on a Tuesday morning. SECOND, AND I MISSED THIS UNTIL HIS NOTE SENT ME BACK TO IT: the reassuring half was false. Ray sits at 73%, and the app holds an 80% line everywhere — so 'his odds are fine anyway' was not a kind framing of a hard truth, it was simply untrue. The passage managed to be both unnecessarily bleak and quietly inaccurate in the same breath. REWRITTEN. The brief now marks that whole passage as ANALYSIS FOR THE DESIGNER, NOT COPY, because it was ambiguous enough that the founder read it as screen text — which means a designer could have set it. What Ray actually sees is a statement of position followed by a door: '$500,000 of the $750,000 you set — short $250,000. Your money lasts in about 7 futures out of 10. Waiting to claim Social Security at 70 takes that to about 8 in 10 — the biggest single change available to you.' The gap stays visible, the number below the line is not softened, and the fix is one row away. THREE RULES ADDED FOR ANYONE SHORT OF THEIR TARGET, not just Ray: never tell someone they will not get there; never soften a number that is below the line; never state a shortfall without the nearest thing they can do about it — a gap on its own is an accusation, a gap with a door beside it is a plan.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; and the check found the sentence was inaccurate as well as unkind.
rows.screens: Ray — the line under his dial was too harsh, AND it was wrong in the reassuring direction

rows.plain: A LIVE, SILENT BUG. The ten-year Treasury yield was being fetched from a feed that had stopped working, and the app quietly used a fallback number instead — so a figure presented as today’s market rate was not. Found only because his mortgage-versus-Treasury comparison depends on that number being real.
rows.means: Found while specifying the founder's mortgage-versus-Treasury comparison, which depends on this number being real. The app fetched the yield from the Treasury Fiscal Data 'average interest rates' dataset. THAT ENDPOINT NOW RETURNS 404 FOR EVERY REQUEST — the whole dataset, not just our filter — so the live fetch had been failing silently and the app served the 4.35% fallback while the actual ten-year sat at 4.63%. Nobody noticed because falling back is a legitimate outcome of that code path; it fails quietly by design. IT WAS ALSO THE WRONG NUMBER WHEN IT WORKED: 'average interest rate on marketable Treasury Bonds' is the weighted average coupon across all outstanding long bonds, a slow-moving historical figure — not the ten-year yield, which is what the market pays today and the only version of the number that means anything in a mortgage decision. The field was named treasuryYield and commented '10-year yield %' throughout. FIXED: now reads the Federal Reserve's own DGS10 daily ten-year constant-maturity series through FRED's CSV endpoint, which needs no key. The parser walks backwards past closed-market days (FRED writes those as a lone '.') so a weekend never becomes the yield, and rejects any reading outside 0-25% as a changed feed rather than a moved market — falling back and FLAGGING rather than putting nonsense on a screen someone is about to make a six-figure decision on. Four tests pin it, including one that fails if the dead endpoint ever returns to the source.

rows.his_words: one critical factor is whether the current mortgage rate is higher or lower than the return on investment or the 10-year yield — if a person pays off the mortgage versus keeping money in a 10-year Treasury, what would be the net saving or cost?
rows.plain: “one critical factor is whether the current mortgage rate is higher or lower than the return on investment or the 10-year yield — if a person pays off the mortgage versus keeping money in a 10-year Treasury.” So the mortgage decision compares your actual mortgage rate against the yield, rather than recommending paying it off on principle.
rows.means: Founder: 'one critical factor is whether the current mortgage rate is higher or lower than the return on investment or the 10-year yield — if a person pays off the mortgage versus keeping money in a 10-year Treasury, what would be the net saving or cost?' Written into brief §3.3.1. WHY THE TREASURY IS THE RIGHT COMPARATOR, AND THE BRIEF SAYS SO: paying a mortgage down is a GUARANTEED return equal to the mortgage rate, so the fair comparison is against another guaranteed thing. Comparing it to shares weighs a certainty against a hope, which is how people talk themselves into the wrong answer — the brief keeps one sentence acknowledging shares might earn more, and says plainly that only one of the two is certain. PAT'S NUMBERS, COMPUTED AND RECONCILING: mortgage 5.50%, ten-year 4.63%, a gap of 0.87 points worth about $3,584 a year at his balance. Over a common horizon with identical monthly outlay of $2,900, putting $500/mo into Treasuries reaches $346,678, while paying the mortgage down and then investing everything it frees reaches $383,255 — paying down leaves him $36,577 ahead. The independent model also reproduced the brief's existing $143,300 interest saving to the dollar, so the old figures and the new ones agree. THREE GUARDS ON IT. Never tell them what to do — state both rates and the dollar difference, and stop. Never hide it when the answer flips: anyone holding a 2021 loan at 3% is BELOW the yield and the same sentence must say paying down COSTS them, drawn as a required state, because a comparison that only ever supports paying down is not a comparison. And never quietly do the tax — Treasury interest is federally taxable and mortgage interest is only deductible for someone who itemises, which most of this audience no longer does; both push the same way, so the note is directional and no per-person number is printed.

rows.plain: He asked what the text would say EXACTLY. It was written out word for word, in the same sentence shape whichever way the comparison falls — so nobody can tell from the layout which answer they are about to get.
rows.means: Founder asked what the text will say exactly. Written verbatim into brief §3.3.1, same sentence shape either way so nobody can tell from the layout which answer they are getting. ABOVE THE YIELD (Pat, 5.5% against 4.63%): 'Your mortgage costs 5.5%. A ten-year Treasury pays 4.63% today. So a dollar into your mortgage saves you more than the same dollar would earn sitting in Treasuries — about $3,584 a year at your balance. Over the life of the loan, paying the extra $500 a month leaves you around $36,577 better off than putting it in Treasuries instead. Shares might earn more than either — or less. Paying the mortgage is the only one that is certain.' BELOW THE YIELD (a 2021 loan at 3.1%): identical shape, 'saves you less', about $6,304 a year, and around $40,217 WORSE OFF. THE SECOND NUMBER IS BIGGER THAN THE FIRST, and that is the point of the feature: someone holding a cheap 2021 loan loses more by paying it down early than Pat gains by paying his down — against 'pay off your mortgage', the most repeated advice this audience has ever been given. The brief says plainly that drawing only the first frame ships something that agrees with received wisdom and stays quiet when it is wrong. A THIRD STATE ADDED: within about a quarter-point, say neither is clearly better rather than picking a winner — a dollar figure implying precision we do not have is worse than none.

rows.his_words: Answer the first question
rows.plain: Two findings on the first screen anyone ever sees. One: the top button read “Answer the first question” without naming what the question was — a button that names no question tells you nothing about what happens when you press it.
rows.means: Two founder findings on the first screen a person ever sees, both confirmed against the handoff and both now brief §5 state 4 and review blocker B8. (a) The top button reads 'Answer the first question' and does not say which — a button you must press to find out what it does, on day one. It becomes 'Add your age'. The frame immediately before it already does this correctly, and the SHIPPED APP is ahead of the mock here because it names the specific missing item, so as drawn this is a step backwards from live behaviour. (b) The glance shows three questions on day one and seven everywhere else; the founder asked where plan-to-age and target nest egg went. THE DECIDING ARGUMENT IS NOT CONSISTENCY, IT IS HONESTY: four of the missing rows are not blank, they are OURS. With nothing answered the app still assumes retire at 65, plan to 90, a 6% return and 2.5% inflation — and the sample gauge on that same frame is computed with them. Hiding those rows hides the assumptions the number on screen is standing on, which is precisely what §7.2 forbids. Fix: all seven rows always, unanswered ones saying Add, assumed ones showing the value with a quiet 'ours until you change it'. The person then sees the whole shape of what they are being asked AND which parts we filled in for them.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; and the assumption-hiding is a rule breach, not just an inconsistency.

rows.his_words: this is assuming the user knows what these odds mean and how to use it — which is not the case 99% of the time.
rows.plain: “this is assuming the user knows what these odds mean and how to use it — which is not the case 99% of the time.” The two hardest screens were rewritten to that instruction: say what the odds mean before showing one.
rows.means: Founder: 'this is assuming the user knows what these odds mean and how to use it — which is not the case 99% of the time.' Brief §5 state 6 and its mirror rewritten to that instruction. WHAT THE ODDS ARE IS NOW SAID ON THE SCREEN, not left to a glossary: 'We play out your retirement 400 times with different market luck. This counts how many of them your money lasted through.' It appears under the number, always — this is precisely where a person meets a percentage that contradicts something else they can see, and without knowing what it counts they cannot resolve it. Both states now read as plain sentences with counts rather than percentages. TWO ERRORS FOUND WHILE REWRITING, BOTH IN THE PASSAGE ITSELF. FIRST: the state said Pat's odds were 45%. That is his ASSETS-VERSUS-TARGET figure against a $2,000,000 target — the other dial. Typing a different target cannot move the odds by a point, so his odds are 48% here as everywhere. On the one state whose entire purpose is stopping two numbers being confused, the brief confused them. SECOND: it instructed the designer to write that 'saving is no longer the lever'. Measured on the engine, Pat saving nothing sits at 45%, at $24,000 a year 64%, at $84,500 a year 90% — saving is an enormous lever. What is true is narrower: he is past his TARGET, so the 'save this much to reach your number' sentence has nothing left to close. That is a sentence losing its job, not a lever disappearing, and telling someone their savings no longer matter would have been false and discouraging at once. The mirror case was verified and holds exactly: a $1,500,000 target is reached by saving $24,000 a year, projecting $1,506,263, with odds of 64%.

rows.plain: “no design created for Goals and Prepare tabs.” Correct — and OUR instruction caused it: the brief said Retire was the only tab being redesigned in this pass, which is the wrong thing to tell a designer when the tabs sit side by side. Goals and Prepare need landing screens too.
rows.means: Founder: 'no design created for Goals and Prepare tabs.' Correct, and OUR instruction caused it — §3.0 said Retire was 'the only one being redesigned in this pass'. That was the wrong thing to write: a three-tab bar where two tabs open onto nothing designed is not a finished design, and a person tapping Prepare on day one has to land somewhere deliberate. Brief §3.0.1 now specifies both landing views and the deliverables list asks for each in a populated AND an empty state. GOALS: the goals themselves with target, progress and on-track state; 'Can I afford it all?' promoted to the front door because with more than one goal that is the real question; the college planner — and the empty state matters more here than anywhere, since most people arrive with no goals set. PREPARE: insurance, estate, tax organiser, build credit, stress test, job safety — mostly things done once, so the useful state is 'not started' or 'done, March 2026' rather than a number; a row saying just 'Estate' tells nobody anything. Both are lopsided against Retire on purpose and the brief says not to pad them for symmetry. SCOPE STATED HONESTLY RATHER THAN ABSORBED: this is a real expansion of the ask, and the designer is told to say so if it does not fit this pass so we can split it, rather than returning one tab drawn and two empty. Logged as blocker B9 — nine now, four of them found by the founder reading the design rather than by my audit.

WHY (from the source): Founder 2026-08-14; two undesigned tabs cannot ship behind a tab bar that offers them.

rows.plain: “how to avoid this in the next brief?” The honest answer is that more care would not have helped — all three errors were written while reading carefully, and two survived several reviews. So every number in a brief is now either computed by a test or explicitly labelled as his own figure, and a test fails the build when a brief and the calculation disagree.
rows.means: Founder: 'how to avoid this in the next brief?' The honest answer is that more care would not have helped — all three errors were written while reading carefully, and two survived several review passes because they looked plausible. A brief is a document full of claims the code can settle, and nothing was settling them. BUILT: src/__tests__/brief_figures_guard.test.ts recomputes every persona figure from the engine and fails the build when the brief and the engine disagree — Pat's $84,500 and where it lands, state 6 and its mirror at $1,506,263 and 64%, June's $4,155 draw and the live spend-more curve at 100% and 80%, Ray's $3,224 and the 73-to-80 move, and the mortgage comparison in both directions. It also asserts the deleted false claim stays deleted. IT CAUGHT TWO THINGS ON ITS FIRST RUN, one a real bug in the test (solveSafeDraw silently returns NaN without the ages) and one a rule too blunt to keep (banning '4.35%' outright failed on the note explaining the dead feed). AND IT SURFACED SOMETHING BIGGER THAN THE THREE ERRORS: PAT'S 48% IS NOT REPRODUCIBLE FROM PAT'S OWN NUMBERS. His four accounts blend to an 8.65% return by the app's own calculation, which puts him at 82% — the 48% only appears at a 5.5% return that appears NOWHERE in the brief. He is the persona the brief opens with and every state is built on him. Recorded in his table as a founder decision with three options (change his holdings, accept 82%, or write down the return we intend) and explicitly NOT resolved by me. The shapes in the brief are unaffected either way, since they concern how the screen behaves rather than which value it holds. FOUR RULES ADDED TO CLAUDE.md: every brief number is engine-computed or labelled founder-stated; any causal claim is measured before it is written; any claim about current behaviour is checked against shipped code, not memory; and a figure with no recorded provenance is a defect even when nobody can prove it wrong. Three guards now exist — orphan routes, the banned word, brief figures — and each caught a real defect within minutes of being written, on surfaces already read carefully by hand.

rows.means: Founder: 'not sure what you want me to check here.' He was right and the framing was mine. I presented three options as a product decision when it was a technical correction: the brief is built end to end around Pat being someone whose plan needs work, so the story was never in question — only the numbers were. FIXED RATHER THAN ESCALATED. Pat's holdings changed, his story did not, and his total stayed at $909,152 so every other figure in the brief still reconciles. He now holds a $380,000 IRA, $379,152 in plain savings, $90,000 in a brokerage and a $60,000 Roth — which the app's own calculation blends to 5.85%, giving him 67% odds. THE NEW MIX IS ALSO THE BETTER TEACHING CASE: 42% of his retirement money sits in a savings account earning about 2.4%, which is extremely common at this age and something the app already has an insight for. His problem is now visible in his own account list instead of hiding inside an unstated assumption. A SECOND MISSING INPUT SURFACED WHILE FIXING THE FIRST: the brief had never said what Pat currently saves, and the mortgage row redirects money FROM saving — so that row could not be computed by anyone reading the brief. It is now $12,000 a year, stated in his table alongside the expected growth, which was also missing. EVERYTHING DOWNSTREAM WAS RECOMPUTED FROM THE ENGINE, NOT ADJUSTED BY HAND: the closing sentence is now $77,500 landing at $2,008,196 with one step lower missing at $1,989,909; the growth breakdown is $426,859 on what he has, $542,500 put in, $129,685 on the new money; state 6 reads 1 future in 3; the mirror is $17,500 reaching $1,505,001 at 74%, so on-target-but-short-of-the-line still holds; the mortgage line is 67 out of 100 to 65 out of 100. Nine guard tests pin all of it. The guard also caught two of my own mistakes today — a probe that silently read default returns because I spread the wrong field names, and two assertions too blunt to tell history from a live figure.

rows.his_words: Ray 64 — see what waiting is worth? Where does that take you, as when should I claim Social Security is below on the same screen.
rows.plain: “Ray 64 — see what waiting is worth? Where does that take you, as when should I claim Social Security is below on the same screen.” The question exposed the defect: the headline carried a link to a decision that was already sitting on the same screen. A headline never carries a door the decisions list already opens.
rows.means: Founder: 'Ray 64 — see what waiting is worth? Where does that take you, as when should I claim Social Security is below on the same screen.' The question exposed the defect: the link and the Social Security row sat a few centimetres apart on one screen — two doors to one place, one above the other, on a surface we have already been told is too busy. And a link that scrolls a short way down the same page is the worst option of all: this audience taps it expecting a new screen and gets what looks like nothing happening. FIXED. The hero now names the lever and says where it is — 'the biggest single thing you could change is when you claim Social Security, it is the first decision below' — with no link. That still honours the rule that a shortfall is never stated without the nearest thing they can do about it: the fix is named AND located, just not linked twice. THE DIVISION OF LABOUR IS NOW STATED AS THE PATTERN FOR THE WHOLE SCREEN: the hero gives a decision's effect on the ODDS (7 in 10 to 8 in 10), the row gives it in DOLLARS ($624 a month). Two useful facts about one decision, each where it belongs — not one sentence printed twice. GENERALISED: the hero never carries a door to something the decisions list already opens; if a hero sentence wants a link, that is a sign the decision belongs in the list and is missing from it. AND IT SETTLED AN OPEN QUESTION ELSEWHERE: §3.4 had been leaving it to the designer whether the dated 'next decision' card should exist or become the first row of the decisions list. The same principle decides it — recommendation is to drop the separate card. That one IS flagged for the founder rather than decided, because the card is built and shipping and a test pins it, so removing it changes something already approved.

rows.his_words: the number you set
rows.plain: Two naming rules, binding on the whole surface. CALL IT THE TARGET NEST EGG — not “the number you set”, not “your target”, not “your number”. One name, so it reads as one thing wherever it appears.
rows.means: Two founder naming rules, both now binding on the whole surface and both in brief §3.5.1. CALL IT THE TARGET NEST EGG: not 'the number you set', not 'your target', not 'your number'. Ray's hero now reads '$500,000 of your $750,000 target nest egg', and the same correction applied to both hard states. The app already uses that exact label in the one place it appears, and it is the wording of the question in §3.2, so the screens agree. COUNT IN FUTURE SIMULATIONS: '7 future simulations out of 10', never '7 futures out of 10'. On its own the word 'futures' reads as though we are making predictions about someone's life; 'future simulations' says plainly that these are runs of a model, which is the entire point of the sentence. Applied to every count in the brief and pinned by the figures guard, which now fails if the bare form returns. A LIVE GAP FOUND WHILE CHECKING THE FIRST RULE AND FLAGGED RATHER THAN FIXED: the shipped app has NO typed target at all. Its 'Target nest egg' row shows a figure WE derive — the pot that would reach 80% odds — so the label is right but the number is ours, not theirs. That is exactly what the founder corrected at the start of this engagement ('target nest egg is a number entered by user'). The redesign introduces the typed value; noting it so the gap is not mistaken for done.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; the words have to say what the number actually is.

rows.his_words: we can enter target number but give them an opportunity to modify it. Add this verbiage to the question.
rows.plain: “we can enter target number but give them an opportunity to modify it. Add this verbiage to the question.” This closes a live hole: the shipped app filled the target in without ever saying it was ours or offering to change it — so our assumption was reading as the person’s own answer.
rows.means: Founder: 'we can enter target number but give them an opportunity to modify it. Add this verbiage to the question.' Written into brief §3.2. THIS CLOSES A LIVE HOLE: the shipped app has a row labelled 'Target nest egg' with a dollar figure the person never typed — the app works it out itself as the pot that reaches 80% odds. So we show someone a number, call it their target, and never mention we picked it. That is the founder's very first correction of this engagement, still live on the tab. THE FIX IS NOT AN EMPTY ROW: a blank target is a worse first experience than a sensible starting figure, since most people genuinely have no number in mind. So we fill it AND say whose it is, inside the question itself — 'What's your target nest egg? $1,250,000 — our starting figure, not yours. Change it to your own number.' For Pat the suggestion is $1,250,000, verified against the engine and pinned; note it sits well BELOW the $2,000,000 he actually typed, which is exactly the point — our suggestion and his ambition are different things and the screen must never blur them. THREE RULES: the row reads as ours until they touch it and as theirs the moment they do, with the qualifier disappearing once they type; changing it never moves the odds (the target is a yardstick, not an input); and it is never shown anywhere without the qualifier, because a suggestion that loses its label on one screen becomes a promise on that screen. Open question 3 in §10 is now answered and struck. THE GUARD CAUGHT MY THIRD MISTAKE OF THE DAY while pinning this: I solved the suggested target without the shared simulation inputs and got $70,000 instead of $1,250,000 — a silently wrong number I would not have spotted by reading.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; the app has been calling its own figure the user's target since before this engagement.

rows.his_words: Can I spend more?
rows.plain: “build it, then audit 10 calculations, 10 features, 10 flows, 10 decisions.” The Plan redesign was built and then audited against 49 checks — the audit is part of the work rather than something that happens if there is time.
rows.means: Founder: build it, then audit 10 calculations, 10 features, 10 flows, 10 decisions. BUILT: the typed target end to end (store field, engine, a field to type it in, and our 80%-odds figure offered as a labelled suggestion while theirs is blank); the second dial; the closing sentence that projects rather than promises and explains that growth does almost half the work; three sub-tabs with Goals and Prepare landings; the mortgage-versus-Treasury comparison on Cash flow Debt in both directions; 'Can I spend more?' answering in place in plain English with every stepper position a live run; the Social Security claim row answering in place; and the dated obligation leading the decisions list. AUDITED, 49 CHECKS, and the audit was written to FIND things rather than to pass: calculations were re-derived independently rather than compared to the app's own helpers, features were rendered and driven rather than grepped, flows were walked end to end, and every decision was traced to shipped code rather than to a document. THREE REAL DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED, all on day one — the first screen anyone sees. (1) Three of the seven questions were asked TWICE, because the work added a second component owning the same seven; that is the identical 'one question, one place' defect the founder found in Ray's hero, on another screen. (2) Retire-at and plan-to showed the app's own defaults with nothing saying they were ours — the same class as the target nest egg the app used to derive and label as theirs. (3) '$0' still printed for what counts and for big costs, which reads as 'you have nothing' rather than 'you haven't told us yet'; the brief named this and it was still shipping. One audit check failed for a NON-defect and is recorded as such: the dated withdrawal row was absent at age 72, which is correct because required withdrawals start at 73 — the audit setup was wrong, not the app. Workbook: docs/FCC-core-55-70/build-audit-plan-redesign-2026-08-14.xlsx. All four audits are committed as tests, so they re-run on every change rather than being a one-day exercise.

rows.his_words: s whole spending figure, inflated, for every year to the horizon — so anyone whose answer included a mortgage was charged it long after the house was paid off. Pat
rows.plain: “we tell the user we include the mortgage payment for the remaining duration — so we state it rather than asking.” The projection now knows a loan payment STOPS when the loan is paid off, instead of carrying it forever, and the app says so rather than asking you to work it out.
rows.means: Founder: we tell the user we include the mortgage payment for the remaining duration — so we state it rather than asking. BUILT, all five pieces. (1) THE SIMULATION NOW KNOWS A PAYMENT STOPS. It charged a person's whole spending figure, inflated, for every year to the horizon — so anyone whose answer included a mortgage was charged it long after the house was paid off. Pat's clears in 2054 and his plan runs to 2058: four years of a payment that will not exist, making his odds pessimistic with no screen saying so. The payment is charged FLAT and never inflated, which is the reason it is a separate field rather than a spending adjustment: a fixed-rate mortgage is the same dollars in 2054 as today, and inflating it for 28 years would overstate it by more than half. (2) WHAT GOES IN CAN VARY BY YEAR, so paying extra is modelled as money not going into savings while the loan runs AND the whole payment freeing up once it clears — both halves, or it is an argument dressed as a calculation. (3) THE EXTRA PAYMENT PERSISTS; it was a text box that forgot the moment you left the screen, so nothing downstream could price it. (4) THE ODDS EFFECT IS TWO FULL RUNS, never a subtraction — the design's placeholder was 67 minus round(extra/500) times 2, a formula that will happily print a number no simulation produced. (5) THE CONSEQUENCE LINE NOW TRAVELS WITH THE CONTROL, which is the gap my own first build left: I moved the mortgage decision to the debt surface and left the retirement effect behind on Retire, exactly the risk the brief named as the whole reason to be careful about the move. TWO CORRECTIONS FOUND WHILE BUILDING: the payoff year rounded UP, putting a 338-month loan in 2055 when its last payment lands October 2054 — a year of a payment that does not exist, on the one figure a person checks against their own statement. And a contribution change dated after retirement does nothing, because there are no contributions then; a mortgage clearing at 79 stops draining savings rather than starting to top them up. Both now pinned. STILL TO DO before the caption can ship: the spending question must stop asking people to include debt payments, or we charge the mortgage twice.
rows.why: Founder 2026-08-14; the caption could not ship while it described something the engine did not do.
rows.screens: ENGINE — a loan payment can now END, savings can vary by year, and the mortgage odds are two real runs

rows.his_words: we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds.
rows.plain: “we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds.” An ETF is one kind of fund, so someone holding a Vanguard mutual fund was reading a label that did not name what they owned. The class is renamed Stocks / Funds.
rows.means: Founder: "we should change ETFs to just Funds to include Mutual funds." ETFs are one kind of fund, and a person holding a Vanguard mutual fund was reading a label that did not name what they own. WHAT CHANGED: the class label everywhere it is shown — the net-worth grouping and its donut, the Performance composition bar, the add-account flow, the itemize picker, and the glossary card, which now reads 'funds — ETFs and mutual funds — that bundle many stocks together'. WHAT THE RENAME EXPOSED, and this matters more than the word: the label was HARDCODED IN EIGHT PLACES instead of read from the one canonical constant, and had already drifted into THREE forms — 'Stocks / ETFs', 'Stocks & ETFs' and 'Stock / ETF' — all reachable in one session. That is the exact failure the calculation module exists to end. A guard now fails the build if any of the dead forms returns (src/__tests__/class_label_guard.test.ts), and it pins the exceptions so it cannot over-reach. WHAT DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE: real product names ('Vanguard S&P 500 ETF' is what that fund is called); the broker-coverage text, which accurately says an institution shares 'stocks, ETFs and mutual funds'; and the internal key `stocks_etf`, which sits in saved user data — renaming that is a migration, not a sweep, and carries risk with no user benefit. Approved mockups still show the old word and were left alone under the never-overwrite-a-mock rule; new mocks use the new label. 1921 tests green, typecheck clean.
rows.why: Founder ruling 2026-08-17. A label that names only one kind of fund misdescribes what half the audience holds.

rows.his_words: s against two people
rows.plain:
The whole income surface redesigned. Six decisions:
1. Base pay becomes a full screen with one expandable section per earner — gross, 401(k), employer match, and what actually lands.
2. A 14-month dated table when pay varies, rather than one typical figure.
3. BOTH earners are captured, not one: a household on $84,000 plus $54,000 was being read as $84,000 — one person’s income against two people’s spending.
4. A filing-status question, which had never been asked, so every couple was taxed as a single filer.
5. Bonus and company shares follow the same who-earns pattern.
6. Interest and dividends are worked out from your holdings rather than asked for, and treated as TAXABLE BUT NOT SPENDABLE.
rows.means: Income redesigned end to end: base pay as a full screen with one expandable section per earner (gross, 401(k), employer match, what lands); a 14-month dated pay table when pay varies; both earners captured, not one; a new filing-status question; bonus and stock follow the same who-earns pattern; interest and dividends calculated from holdings rather than asked, and treated as TAXABLE BUT NOT SPENDABLE.
rows.why: The app grossed up a typed take-home figure and taxed it back down, removing the 401(k) twice ($1,467/mo adrift). Nobody had ever set a filing status, so every couple was taxed as a single filer ($328–$866/mo). The household income was one person's against two people's spending. Dividends were counted as money you can spend when they are reinvested ($250/mo). Findings B27, B30–B35.

rows.plain: Fifteen calculations were each written in two or more places; now none is. 560 calculations, 560 distinct names. A second copy of a calculation cannot be fixed by fixing the first — which is how the same defect kept coming back.

rows.why: Onboarding taxed the full gross and took the 401(k) off afterwards; every other screen used the income grid, where a traditional contribution comes off BEFORE tax. $6,400 in onboarding against $6,560 everywhere else on the employedPartner persona — $160 a month, and only for a household with a partner. It is finding B05 again: B05 was fixed in the grid earlier the same day and never reached this copy. A second implementation cannot be fixed by fixing the first.

rows.plain: Months are keyed by their actual date rather than by position — “2026-07”, not “slot 7 of twelve”. The twelve-slot version wrote January into the wrong year whenever the twelve months crossed a New Year.
rows.means: New src/domain/income/salary-months.ts (MK-CF-F-163..170) with 9 laws. salaryByMonth is now a keyed table ('2026-07' -> amount); an older twelve-slot array is still READ, as the calendar year the person is in now. salaryGrossByMonth, CashFlowScreen, IncomeSetupSheet and the onboarding month grid all go through it. A month the table does not mention falls back to the typical month, never to $0. 237 suites, 2,415 tests green.
rows.why: A fourteen-month window running from last month crosses a year boundary, and slot 0 cannot mean both January and July. It also fixed a live defect: in the rolling frame a chip labelled JAN 27 wrote slot 0, which the domain read back as January of THIS year — the label said one year and the store meant another, and a slot carries no year to disagree with. Annual salary is unmoved on every persona (hourlyServer still $26,400).

rows.his_words: Who earns this income? You / Partner / Both
rows.plain: A spouse’s wage becomes its own block, using the SAME field names as your own, and the household total sums every earner. A household on $84,000 plus $54,000 had been read as $84,000 — one person’s income against two people’s spending.
rows.means: New src/domain/income/earners.ts (MK-CF-F-172..176, 8 laws): the partner's wage is its own block under the SAME field names as the person's own. MK-CF-F-060 salaryGrossByMonth now sums every earner, and employerMatchMonthly does too (MK-CF-F-177 wageGrossByMonth, MK-CF-F-178 wageMatchMonthly answer for one wage). MK-CF-O-001 basePay is the household orchestrator over a list of earners and shows the band on one wage and on all of them; MK-CF-F-171 earnerPay answers for one person. PlanHubScreen, CashFlowScreen and onboarding Summary now read the household. 239 suites, 2,427 tests green.
rows.why: The app asked 'Who earns this income? You / Partner / Both', stored the answer, and kept ONE salary — choosing 'Both' tagged a single wage as belonging to two people. Finding B32. Only MK-CF-F-060 changed: salaryAnnual sums it, MK-CF-F-084 reads that, MK-CF-F-090 reads THAT, so the band comes off both incomes with nothing above it touched. Three screens showed one person's wage as the household's — and the plan's income figure also only annualised monthly pay, so a fortnightly earner's plan was built on a fortnight.

rows.plain: Every “today” in the app is the person’s OWN calendar day, not the day in universal time. Converting local midnight to universal time moves the date back a day anywhere east of Greenwich — which made every look-back answer “nothing” on a device set to India time.
rows.means: Every 'today' stamp in src/ now uses MK-ST-F-065 isoLocalDate (or monthKey): 15 production files, 13 test files. rows.why: new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10) reads as today and is not — after about 5pm in California it already says tomorrow. An expense logged on the evening of the 31st was filed in the next month, a balance was stamped with a date the person had not reached, and a funded-this-month flag flipped a day early. It was in 35 places; only two were declared helpers the one-name guard could see, so the new guard checks the CALL rather than the name.
